title: 5 Best GitHub Repositories for AI Agent Skills
abstract: 5 Best GitHub Repositories for AI Agent Skills Explore five popular AI agent skill collections that help coding agents plan, test, debug, review, and build better software. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on October 21, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode have become very good at writing code. But software engineering is much more than that. You still need to understand requirements, plan features, write tests, debug problems, review changes, and know when something is ready to ship. This is where AI agent skills come in. They are reusable instructions and workflows that teach agents how to handle specific tasks without you having to explain the same process every time. In this article, we will look at five popular open-source collections: Superpowers by Jesse Vincent (⭐285.5K) Skills for Real Engineers by Matt Pocock (⭐260.1K) ECC by Affaan (⭐256.7K) Awesome LLM Apps by Shubham Saboo (⭐137.3K) Agent Skills by Addy Osmani (⭐93.6K) Each takes a slightly different approach to making coding agents more useful for real software development. 1. Superpowers by Jesse Vincent Superpowers is one of the most popular agent skill projects on GitHub. Created by Jesse Vincent and the team at Prime Radiant, it is a software development methodology for coding agents, built from a collection of reusable skills. The important word here is methodology . Instead of simply giving your agent more abilities, Superpowers changes how it approaches software development . Its skills cover things like: brainstorming implementation planning test-driven development systematic debugging Git worktrees parallel agents code review verification For example, if you ask the agent to build a feature, it first uses brainstorming to understand what you actually want. After the design is approved, it creates a plan, implements it using subagents or plan execution, follows test-driven development (TDD), reviews the code, and verifies everything before finishing the branch. Debugging follows the same idea. The systematic-debugging skill uses a structured root-cause process instead of letting the agent randomly change code until something works. This is what makes Superpowers interesting. You are not just installing another prompt or tool. You are basically giving your coding agent a proper software development process . For Claude Code, you can install it with: /plugin install superpowers@claude-plugins-official It also supports Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot CLI, Kimi Code, Antigravity, and several other coding environments. 2. Skills for Real Engineers by Matt Pocock Matt Pocock takes a slightly different approach with Skills for Real Engineers , a collection of agent skills he says he uses every day for real engineering, not vibe coding . Instead of trying to control the entire development process, the skills are designed to be small, adaptable, and composable . You can use the ones you need and combine them into your own workflow. Some of the most useful include: grill-me grill-with-docs to-spec to-tickets implement tdd diagnosing-bugs code-review research domain-modeling improve-codebase-architecture handoff One of my favorites is grill-with-docs . Instead of letting the agent guess what you want, it interviews you about the change while building a shared domain model, improving terminology, and updating project documents such as CONTEXT.md and ADRs. Then you have skills like tdd , which follows the classic red-green-refactor loop, and diagnosing-bugs , which gives the agent a structured debugging process instead of letting it randomly try fixes. For larger work, you can even build a workflow like: grill-with-docs → to-spec → to-tickets → implement → code-review The repository itself documents this as its main multi-session development chain. You can install the skills with: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills The installer lets you choose which skills you want and which coding agents to install them on. It copies the files into your project, so you can edit them to match the way you like to work. Matt recommends also installing and running setup-matt-pocock-skills once for each repo. If Superpowers feels like installing a complete engineering methodology, Matt Pocock's collection feels more like borrowing the workflows of an experienced engineer and picking the ones that work for you . 3. ECC by Affaan ECC by Affaan Mustafa is the biggest collection in this list in terms of raw capabilities. It goes beyond a normal folder of SKILL.md files and combines skills, specialized agents, rules, hooks, memory, continuous learning, security tools, and integrations for different coding agents . The current repository includes: 292 skills 68 specialized agents 94 command shims memory across sessions continuous learning AgentShield security scanning Its skills cover TDD, research, frontend development, machine learning, security, operations, architecture, testing, and agent orchestration. Affaan describes its workflow like this: plan → test → implement → review → verify → remember → improve The last two steps are what make it interesting. ECC can preserve useful context across sessions and turn repeated patterns into reusable skills and learned behaviors. It also includes AgentShield , which scans agent configurations for things like secrets, risky permissions, hooks, MCP settings, and prompt-related security issues. You can install it with: npx ecc-universal@2.2.1 setup Or use the guided installer: npx ecc-universal@2.2.1 install --guided Claude Code currently has the strongest integration, with support for Codex and varying levels of support for Cursor, OpenCode, Kimi Code, Gemini, and other coding agents. ECC is probably overkill if you only need a better debugging prompt. But if you want your coding agent setup to behave more like a complete engineering platform with memory, security, and specialized workers , it is one of the most ambitious options available. 4. Awesome LLM Apps by Shubham Saboo Shubham Saboo's Awesome LLM Apps is a little different from the other repositories on this list. Instead of focusing only on skills, it contains 100+ open-source AI agents, agent skills, and RAG applications built around models such as GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Llama, and Qwen. That broader scope is what makes it interesting. You can see how agents, tools, retrieval, multiple models, and skills are actually combined into working applications. Its Agent Skills collection includes: Project Graveyard : finds abandoned projects and helps decide which one is worth finishing Scope Creep Detector : checks whether a code change has grown beyond its original goal Commit Archaeologist : uses Git history to understand why code exists Self-Improving Agent Skills : automatically tests and improves agent skills Advisor Orchestrator Worker : splits larger tasks across an orchestrator, advisor, and workers For example, you can install Project Graveyard with: npx skills add https://github.com/Shubhamsaboo/awesome-llm-apps/tree/main/agent_skills/project-graveyard It scans your local Git repositories, looks at their history, identifies why projects were abandoned, and suggests which one may be worth bringing back. 5. Agent Skills by Addy Osmani Addy Osmani's Agent Skills focuses more directly on production software engineering. The collection organizes its workflows around six stages: DEFINE → PLAN → BUILD → VERIFY → REVIEW → SHIP It currently contains 24 skills covering requirements, planning, TDD, frontend development, API design, debugging, security, performance, code review, CI/CD, observability, documentation, and shipping. There are also lifecycle commands such as /spec , /plan , /build , /test , /review , and /ship , which load the appropriate workflows for each stage. One part I particularly like is its focus on quality gates .

title: Physicist Christopher Stubbs joins Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust
abstract: Dr. Christopher Stubbs, an experimental physicist and former Dean of Science at Harvard University, has joined Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust. He brings to the Trust decades of scientific expertise across observational cosmology and precision measurement. He has also advised the US government on national security and arms control. “I am honored to join Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust and to help the company deliver on its public benefit mission,” said Stubbs. “I use AI tools in my research every day and see what they make possible, and as an educator I have confronted some of the hard questions they raise. As a grandfather, I want to help ensure that AI is developed and deployed for the long-term benefit of humanity.” Stubbs is the Samuel C. Moncher Professor of Physics and of Astronomy at Harvard, where he served as Dean of Science from 2018 to 2024. In 1998, as a member of the High-Z Supernova Search Team, he helped discover the accelerating expansion of the universe, work that later earned the team the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics. He was also the inaugural project scientist for what is now the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which started a 10-year survey of the southern sky in June. One of its aims is to study the accelerating expansion he helped discover. More recently, he’s written about how to keep AI-assisted research reproducible when models can give different answers to the same question. He’s a member of JASON, an independent group of scientists who have advised the US government on defense and technology since 1960. “When Chris found evidence that the universe was expanding at a rate no one expected, he and his team followed the data even when it went against the prevailing wisdom of the field. As AI starts to transform how science itself is done, Chris’s intellectual honesty, rigor, and commitment to the truth are the values we want shaping the future of this technology, and I’m grateful he’s bringing his deep expertise to the Trust,” said Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President of Anthropic. Anthropic is a Public Benefit Corporation, which means we’re structured to balance commercial growth with our public benefit purpose. The Trust exists to help us hold that balance over the long term. It has the authority to appoint a majority of Anthropic’s board, and Trustees advise the board and our leadership on critical decisions, particularly those involving risks and societal impacts of AI. This week we published our first Public Benefit Report , a public account of how we’re working toward our charter and where we’re falling short. The Trustees helped define the five charter pillars it measures us against, and the report closes with their assessment of our progress to date. Subject to stockholder approval, we’ve also committed to setting aside a portion of Anthropic’s shares to Anthropic Public Benefit Fund , a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. “Helping the world build powerful AI safely and making sure it meaningfully improves people’s lives both depend on a deep understanding of science and on leading with integrity,” added Neil Buddy Shah, Chair of the Long-Term Benefit Trust. “Not only has Chris worked on some of the hardest problems in science, but he has consistently been a high-integrity leader of large, complex, collaborative scientific endeavors across academia, government, and the national laboratories. That will be of great value to the Trust as we support Anthropic in developing AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.” Stubbs, the Trust’s first physicist, joins Shah, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and former Federal Reserve Chair Ben Bernanke. Trustees are independent of the company’s management and investors.

title: HCLTech joins the Claude Partner Network as a Global Premier partner
abstract: Anthropic is partnering with HCLTech (opens in new tab) , a global technology company with more than 230,000 people in 60 countries. HCLTech will build agentic solutions on Claude for its clients through a dedicated Anthropic Business Unit and Center of Excellence, embed Claude in HCLSoftware products, and integrate Claude and Claude Code into AI Force, the platform it uses to run IT services for clients. HCLTech becomes a Global Premier Partner (opens in new tab) in the Claude Partner Network. HCLTech provides solutions for financial services, manufacturing, life sciences and healthcare, technology, semiconductor, telecom and media, retail and CPG, and mobility and public services. In these environments, a mistake is expensive and every change needs to be reviewed, logged, and approved. The partnership is built to put Claude into that work with the controls designed for those environments. How HCLTech is putting Claude to work HCLTech is bringing Claude into its business in three places and is designing each with guardrails and human review. A dedicated Anthropic Business Unit and Center of Excellence. HCLTech’s forward-deployed engineers will set up secure sandbox environments where clients can test Claude against their own systems and data before deploying. The Center will train client workforces, help engineering teams adopt AI-native practices, and build the organizational controls for running agents safely at scale. Claude inside HCLSoftware products. HCLSoftware becomes an Anthropic independent software vendor (ISV) partner and will embed Claude in select products across cybersecurity, automation, business process applications, and application development. The first are HCL BigFix for endpoint management, HCL AppScan for application security testing, and the Actian AI analyst for data and analytics. Claude and Claude Code in AI Force. AI Force is how HCLTech delivers IT support, code remediation, and digital employee services for the enterprises it serves. Claude and Claude Code go into that platform with policy guardrails, exception handling, and human oversight for high-impact changes. Agents handle the routine work, and HCLTech engineers review and approve anything that touches a client’s production systems. “Few technology companies combine the scale of a global systems integrator with the product depth of an ISV,” says C Vijayakumar, CEO and Managing Director at HCLTech. “That gives us a rare advantage to securely engineer and deploy Agentic AI at scale and deliver the business outcomes that matter most to our clients. Our partnership with Anthropic further strengthens our capabilities to achieve the same.” "AI can only be as useful as it is trustworthy, and we build Claude to give companies the confidence to bring it into their most sensitive and valuable work,” says Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President at Anthropic. “HCLTech manages those kinds of systems for banks, hospitals, telecom companies and manufacturers, and we’re excited to partner with them as they integrate Claude and Claude Code. This partnership — and our broader commitment to advancing capability and safety together — is how AI will change the way entire industries run for the better.” To learn more about working with Anthropic partners, visit the Claude Partner Network (opens in new tab) .

title: Claude Security now scans continuously and tracks fixes
abstract: Since Claude Security entered public beta in April, thousands of organizations have used it to find over a million vulnerabilities. Instead of waiting for someone to start a scan, Claude Security now keeps up with your repositories as your code changes, keeps track of which findings get fixed, and uses what your team tells it about your environment to decide what matters. Claude Security is powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos, with no Cyber Verification Program access required. The latest version of Claude Security is available today in public beta for Claude Enterprise customers. Organizations receive $25,000 in free usage credits each month, for two months. The offer applies to usage through December 31, 2026. You can view full terms in the Help Center . Continuous monitoring keeps up with your code A scan captures one moment, and code changes every day. Teams told us they wanted coverage that stays current without anyone having to schedule it. Create a project, connect your repositories through the Claude GitHub app (including GitHub Enterprise Server) or with an access token from GitLab and other Git providers, and choose the branch and scope for each. Claude runs a deep baseline scan, then scans changes regularly based upon their risk and complexity, so your list of findings stays close to the current state of your code. A project can hold multiple repositories, so Claude can catch issues that live between services, like a backend that trusts input a client was supposed to validate. Findings are marked fixed when the fix ships Most fixes happen outside the tool that found the issue. Claude Security checks open findings against the code that changed and marks them fixed when the fix lands, whether your team fixed it in Claude Code or in a separate process. If Claude Security finds the issue again later, the finding reopens automatically. Your team’s knowledge shapes the scan Every environment has controls a scanner can’t see from the code alone. Teams wanted a way to tell Claude Security about those controls, and to look across services that depend on each other. Now, each project has a knowledge base where you can describe how your code is deployed, which security policies apply, and anything a new security engineer on your team would need to know. Claude Security also generates a threat model from your code that your team can review and edit. Subsequent scans use those threat models to decide what’s worth flagging. Added context also helps Claude Security skip risks your environment already handles. Severity and exploit paths for every finding Each finding comes with a severity rating, judged against your project’s threat model, and an explanation of how an attacker could reach the vulnerable code, so teams can fix what’s actually reachable first. Findings can include a diagram of the attack path. Findings reach your tools, with controls for larger rollouts The new API lets you integrate Claude Security into your existing workflows. You can list and read projects and findings, resolve or reopen findings, and create and manage projects and their repositories. Users can create a personal access token in Claude Security settings, and it can only see and change what the user can. Webhooks can also notify your systems when a new finding lands. Claude Security is also available as an MCP connector in Claude.ai and Claude Code. An engineer can pull up a finding, ask Claude about it, start the fix, and mark it resolved in the same session. New role-based access controls let admins decide who can view projects, triage findings, and create projects. Organizations can open Claude Security to more teams that own the code without giving everyone access to create projects. Getting started The latest version of Claude Security is available in public beta for Claude Enterprise customers starting today. Admins can enable it in the admin console and set who on their team can access it. Organizations receive $25,000 in free usage credits each month, for two months. The offer applies to usage through December 31, 2026.
