title: Introducing Claude Duet
abstract: Today, we’re opening a research preview of Claude Duet, a new app where Claude works as a proactive agent. It comes to you with what needs your attention, completes tasks you ask of it, keeps working even when you step away, and checks with you before it acts on your behalf. We built Claude Duet for professionals and small business owners with more on their plates than they can track. It’s available as a standalone app on iOS and Android, and on claude.ai. For this research preview, Claude Duet is included in Pro and Max plans and uses the same usage limits as the rest of Claude. To get access, join the waitlist (opens in new tab) . Put your attention where it matters most We designed Claude Duet to be a partner you can trust. Professionals of all kinds have to juggle many decisions a day, and we think they’ll find Claude Duet most useful. It helps you prioritize where to spend your time and energy, and to leave room for the ambitious projects that felt impossible or daunting before. What makes Claude Duet so helpful is its judgment. We designed it around Claude Opus 5.5 (opens in new tab) and built it to be resourceful and to decide what needs you, what can wait, and when to check with you first. Each morning, it sends you a short brief on the most important items across your connected apps. Throughout the day, it keeps tabs on those apps and messages you only when something needs your attention. You can also hand it tasks of all shapes—from simple administrative tasks of scheduling meetings to more complex ones, such as building dashboards with dozens of tools, creating financial or sales forecasts, prototyping, and building web apps. Safety and discretion are built in Claude Duet draws on years of security, safety, and privacy work on agents, both our own and the infrastructure businesses use to run theirs: Claude Duet draws on our framework for trustworthy agents (opens in new tab) , which also guides agents like Claude Code and Claude in Chrome. Claude Duet’s handling of credentials follows the design we use for Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab) , so it never directly sees your passwords or sign-in tokens. Actions are approved by our auto mode classifier (opens in new tab) , the same safeguard that protects Claude and Claude Code from taking steps you didn’t ask for. Claude Duet’s defenses against hidden instructions and prompt injection come from our browser-use research (opens in new tab) , and our models and safeguards also cover this more broadly. We run adversarial tests for Claude Duet’s security infrastructure. Red teams and an external firm penetration tested Claude Duet, and it’s covered by our public bug bounty program (opens in new tab) . How Duet handles sensitive information. We’re also releasing Claude Duet with a new dedicated classifier and safety system prompt that checks each message and guards against leaks of sensitive information. An agent that reads email and sends messages for you is constantly deciding where information should go. This new classifier and prompt are designed to reject requests to share the strictest tier of information, including credit card numbers and government identification. Other sensitive information, such as health or personal finances, are let through only when you’ve explicitly instructed Claude Duet to send it. We’re continuing to develop and strengthen these protections, and will share more details about how Claude Duet is designed for safety in the coming days. How testers are using Claude Duet People at Anthropic have been using Claude Duet to accomplish more, but also to leave more room for thinking and being present. Boris Cherny, who leads our Claude Code team, talks through his mental to-do list with Claude Duet on walks, instead of saving the work for his desk. Chelsea Larsson, who leads our model and product behavior design team, hands Claude Duet her to-do list before leaving to be with her kids and it saves the results for an evening report. And the team behind Claude Duet uses it to build the product. Karan Ahuja, who leads the team, works with it to schedule user interviews, partner with him on prototypes, and even ship code. We gave small business owners and entrepreneurs early access to Claude Duet, and some have been using it to help run their businesses. Here’s what some of them said: “Jess gets a rundown from Claude Duet each morning. One day, without being asked, it flagged a property showing that was on her calendar for the wrong day. “[This is] exactly the kind of thing I want caught without having to ask,” she said.” Jess Provencher, broker and owner, Pro Homes “Amin owns Shahs of Kabob in South Florida with about 110 employees. He’s used Claude Duet for accounting, customer support, and marketing, and has worked through his invoices store by store. “It brings it all together,” he said. “I don’t need to open up 100 tabs.” Amin Ebrahimi, owner, Shahs of Kabob “Mya Dalton, a brand strategist, had a call coming up with a potential client. Claude Duet saw it on her calendar and prepared a brief. It also noticed the call fell right before her flight and offered to move it. “I didn’t realize that it was right before my flight,” she said. “I love that proactivity.” Mya Dalton, a brand strategist How Claude Duet works Your context from Claude is the foundation. Claude Duet carries over your memory, skills, and connected apps from your Claude account, so setting it up requires minimal work. What changes is how you work together: Claude Duet comes to you first, and you can message it through typing or voice in one ongoing thread, so a quick reply and a weeklong project both start in the same place. Work continues when you step away. Claude Duet has a virtual machine with its own browser, so it doesn’t require your laptop or phone to be on. Describe a task in a short message, and it works out which apps to use and what steps to take in the background. You’ll receive a notification when the task is complete or needs your review. Receive a message when something needs you. Claude Duet checks your connected accounts every few hours, because checking nonstop would use up your plan’s limits much faster. We’re continuing to test its judgment about when to message you, and we’ll keep tuning it based on what testers tell us. You can also tell it what you want to hear about and how often. Important decisions stay with you. Claude Duet reads, drafts, and prepares work on its own. But before it sends a message, makes a payment, signs a document, or deletes anything, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your approval. A few things are off-limits even with your approval, like trading securities or moving money between accounts. You’re also able to disconnect any app Claude Duet has access to. Connect with the tools your business runs on. Claude Duet can use the over 6,000 connectors and plugins in the Claude Marketplace (opens in new tab) to: Find the Gmail and Slack messages you’ve missed and help you reply. Check Intuit QuickBooks or Stripe for unpaid invoices and draft reminders. Prepare and run payroll in Gusto, with hours, bonuses, and reimbursements filled in. Draft a job posting and, once you edit and approve, post it to LinkedIn. Help prepare agreements and send them for review and signature through Docusign. Draft follow-up emails using the contact and deal history in HubSpot. Turn your product launch into a social campaign in Canva. Set up, design, and manage your Shopify store. Coming soon, a richer visual editor will let you design your storefront and preview it before anything goes live. You can also use Claude Duet to purchase things for your business using Link, Stripe’s digital wallet. Claude Duet confirms the item with you, and Link asks you to approve the spend. It then pays with a virtual card, so your real card number isn’t shared. It can also use Shop Pay from Shopify to check out at online stores.

title: Design Proteins with RFD4-Proteina Using Reward-Guided Inference-Time Search
abstract:
Protein design is a search problem. Choose amino acids for an eight-residue protein sequence and more than 25 billion combinations are possible. Choose amino acids for a 100-residue protein sequence and the number of possibilities exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe. Somewhere in that space is a protein that opens a path to a new therapy. There are too many combinations to search exhaustively, so finding it depends on knowing where to look. RFD4-Proteina , an NVIDIA BioNeMo open model co-developed with the Institute for Protein Design at the University of Washington’s School of Medicine, navigates that space using patterns learned from nature. It co-designs protein sequences and all-atom structures, and uses reward-guided inference-time search to focus compute on the most promising candidates. This tutorial shows computational biologists, ML engineers and drug discovery researchers how to design protein binder candidates against PD-L1, an oncology target, using reward-guided inference-time search and introduces experimental validation results across design tasks. You can access RFD4-Proteina in two ways: Choose the open model for training, inference, method development, and direct control over sampling code or Choose the NIM microservice for rapid inference deployment with an HTTP interface Building on Proteina-Complexa ’s partially latent approach, RFD4-Proteina combines explicit backbone coordinates with latent representation, learned sequence and atomistic variables. Its autoencoder decoder produces the sequence and all-atom structure together, removing the separate inverse-folding handoff to a model such as ProteinMPNN . Prerequisites Open model Supported Linux GPU host and Python 3.12; follow the repository setup guide and use a supported NVIDIA GPU. Model cache: Setup downloads the Hugging Face bundle automatically; set HF_HOME only if you want a different cache directory. NIM Self-host: x86_64 or arm64 Linux meeting the NIM prerequisites , Docker, NVIDIA Driver, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and an NGC API key . NIM API endpoint (not recommended for production runs): HTTP access through NVIDIA build.nvidia.com via Shell and Python scripts, no local GPU or model installation required. About RFD4-Proteina Figure 1. RFD4-Proteina uses molecular context, design constraints, and design regions to generate protein sequences and all-atom structures, with optional reward-guided search to guide generation The search loop shown in Figure 1, above, is where RFD4-Proteina focuses its compute. During inference-time reasoning search, the model denoises generation trajectories to obtain structures, scores these designs, retains and branches promising partial states, and continues until the generation criteria are reached. Rewards can measure geometry, interactions, or independent prediction confidence. This kind of extra search optimizes designs against a specified objective to yield higher-scoring designs. Later in this tutorial, you will see how a user can enable this functionality through the open model and the NIM. RFD4-Proteina is faster and uses less memory than RFD3 for several reasons: It works on a residue-level latent representation instead of atom-level, which avoids memory blow-up. Engineering of the diffusion process cuts sampling from about 400 steps in Proteina-Complexa to 60, and computation is concentrated on the parts of the process that matter most thanks to reasoning capabilities in the model. Inference-time search is also faster, since the oracles (OF3 and physics methods like tmol ) are CUDA-accelerated. The model and kernels were co-designed with the cuEquivariance and BioNeMo Inference Runtime (BIR) teams for speed and scalability. Figure 2. At 200 residues, RFD4-Proteina delivers 3.8x faster generation and uses 84% leeds peak reserved memory than RFD3 in the reported generation benchmark From a molecular design idea to candidate designs Figure 3. The reference workflow links molecular design, computational evaluation, and experimental testing in an iterative cycle The workflow in Figure 3, above, demonstrates how to use RFD4-Proteina to go from a scientific objective to candidates for experimental testing. An agent can coordinate these tools and track results, while scientists define the objectives and use experimental evidence to guide the next round. Preparing the molecular inputs and environment Begin by defining the criteria and requirements for generation. For example, RFD4-Proteina expects users to define what may change, what must remain fixed, and computational and experimental success criteria. Use AtomWorks to generate /manipulate the input data. AtomWorks is the molecular data layer used to prepare structures and design annotations for RFD4-Proteina. Its Python and PyMOL workflows prepare fixed atoms, designable residues, hotspots, and molecular context. Preserve the supplied ligand or motif chemistry when designing surrounding protein. Both the open model and NIM accept annotated CIFs or a condition specification plus its source structure. The specification below fixes the target and defines the new binder. The repository’s cropped PD-L1 structure from PDB 5O45 serves as the target. Fix the target’s sequence and backbone coordinates, allow its side chains to repack, and direct binder generation toward hotspot atoms on Tyr56, Met115, and Tyr123. The new binder has 100–150 residues, with free sequence and coordinates. Clone the repository, then run the examples from its root. This writes pdl1.json ; both paths use the same target CIF and conditions. git clone https://github.com/RosettaCommons/RFD4-Proteina.git
cd RFD4-Proteina cat > pdl1.json <<'JSON'
{ "pdl1_binder": { "input": "docs/examples/inputs/5o45_cropped.cif", "contig": "100-150, /0, A17-131", "conditions": { "C_CRD": {"true": [{"select": "sel('A') and is_protein_backbone"}]}, "C_SEQ": {"true": [{"select": "sel('A')"}]}, "C_HOT": {"true": [ {"select": "sel('A/*/56/[CG,OH]')"}, {"select": "sel('A/*/115/[CG,SD]')"}, {"select": "sel('A/*/123/[CD2,OH]')"} ]} } }
}
JSON Open model setup On a supported Linux/CUDA system, install the repository environment with a current uv release (validated with 0.12.24). If uv is already installed, update it first so it recognizes CUDA 13.2. Setup caches the Hugging Face model bundle, including the paired autoencoder. While the model repository is private, authenticate with hf auth login using an account with access. bash setup.sh --native
source .venv/bin/activate NIM environment setup To host the NIM, run this block in Bash on a supported GPU host with Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit installed. read -rsp 'NGC API key: ' NGC_API_KEY; echo
export NGC_API_KEY
printf '%s' "$NGC_API_KEY" | docker login nvcr.io \ -u '$oauthtoken' --password-stdin
image=nvcr.io/nim/ipd/rfd4-proteina:latest
docker pull "$image"
export RFD4_NIM_IMAGE="$(docker image inspect \ --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' "$image")"
printf '%s\n' "$RFD4_NIM_IMAGE" > nim-image.txt
export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE="$HOME/.cache/nim"
mkdir -p "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE"
docker run -d --rm --name rfd4-proteina \ --runtime=nvidia --gpus 'device=0' -p 8000:8000 \ -e NGC_API_KEY -v "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE":/opt/nim/.cache \ --shm-size=16g "$RFD4_NIM_IMAGE" Generate sequences and structures Open-model generation Save the following as design.py in the repository root. The same script supports generation and search. Proteina.from_pretrained("nvidia/RFD4-Proteina") loads the current Hugging Face model and paired autoencoder checkpoints. import hydra
from rfd4_proteina import Proteina
from rfproteina.generate import run_generation @hydra.main(config_path="configs", config_name="inference", version_base="1.3")
def main(cfg): model = Proteina.from_pretrained("nvidia/RFD4-Proteina") run_generation(cfg, model=model) if __name__ == "__main__": main() Generate one candidate from the repository root: python design.py inputs=pdl1.

title: Inside NVIDIA Sentry: Secure AI Agents at Runtime
abstract: An AI agent can complete its assignment and still cross a security boundary. Recent incidents show that agents can circumvent security controls while using tools, credentials, and services to pursue their assigned goals. Monitoring and enforcement need to operate outside the agent’s reach so that it can’t alter or disable them. NVIDIA Sentry is a security software framework that monitors AI agents and enforces policies governing their access to models, tools, and data. Part of the NVIDIA OpenShell reference architecture announced at GTC Berlin, it’s built on NVIDIA DOCA , runs on NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs , and provides host-isolated runtime protection for AI agents. NVIDIA Sentry validates that an agent operates according to its designed intent and within its defined operational boundaries. Trusted even when host resources can’t be trusted, it controls the agent’s only path to the model, providing tamper-evident traceability of agent activity while enforcing granular security controls on agent access in silicon. In addition to inspecting agent communications, NVIDIA Sentry uses out-of-band observability to establish real-time situational awareness, continuously evaluating agents’ runtime security and behavior to validate their security and integrity. This post explains how NVIDIA Sentry evaluates agent requests, detects threats, and enforces security policies independently of host software. An independent security layer for agent runtime protection An earlier agentic AI security post described how NVIDIA BlueField runs security services in a hardware trust domain independent from the host. NVIDIA Sentry builds on that foundation to continuously monitor AI agent behavior and enforce access policies independently of host software, establishing a strict security boundary in a separate hardware trust domain outside the agent’s reach to keep agents operating within their designed intent. Software runtime boundaries remain essential. NVIDIA OpenShell is a secure runtime for autonomous agents that governs what an agent can do. OpenShell separates policy enforcement from the agent workload, so a compromised agent can’t change its own restrictions. NVIDIA Sentry adds an independent hardware safeguard out of band, running on BlueField-4, beyond the agent’s reach and knowledge. In the OpenShell reference architecture, agents execute on NVIDIA Vera CPUs , while BlueField-4 sits on the node’s only path to the model. NVIDIA Sentry inspects agent-to-model communications and enforces access policies without relying on the agent to report its own behavior. Memory introspection adds context about the agent’s execution environment, such as a container or microVM, to help detect external threats and agent misbehavior. Governing agent communications DOCA Tower is NVIDIA Sentry’s AI security gateway. Built on Envoy , the open source edge and service proxy, it operates as a transparent proxy for agent traffic, placing a bidirectional inspection layer between an agent and the external environment. Agent network traffic reaches BlueField-4 through a direct network I/O path that bypasses host OS/hypervisor packet processing. All of the agent’s network communications are governed by NVIDIA Sentry as BlueField-4 sits on the only path to the model and to the outside world. An agent’s network access boundary is controlled using DOCA Flow and DOCA Tower, which work in concert to restrict agent access to approved resources. DOCA Flow is used to implement a layer-4 firewall for each agent, accelerated in silicon on BlueField-4. The firewall blocks connections to unauthorized destinations and forwards permitted traffic to DOCA Tower for layer-7 (application layer) inspection, authorization, and additional security checks. DOCA Tower acts as a transparent proxy, performing Transport Layer Security (TLS) termination using built-in, in-silicon TLS acceleration. For connections configured for inspection, it decrypts the agent traffic permitted by the layer-4 firewall to inspect and control agent communications. NVIDIA Sentry uses the Open Policy Agent (OPA), an open source policy engine, to evaluate access requests against defined policies. OPA uses Rego, a declarative domain-specific language designed to evaluate complex hierarchical data structures. OPA runs locally in memory and can evaluate requests in under a millisecond, depending on policy complexity and configuration. DOCA Tower is compatible with OpenShell policies, using OPA to extend network access policies and runtime controls into BlueField-4 and to the infrastructure. Figure 1. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower to inspect access requests and a policy engine to evaluate authorization, with runtime context from DOCA Argus Enforcing agent access policies with runtime context An agent’s network communications provide only part of the information needed to assess its security and integrity. Visibility into the agent’s execution environment adds context for evaluating access requests that go beyond a traditional resource access policy. DOCA Argus provides real-time visibility into an agent’s execution environment and operational state, giving NVIDIA Sentry additional context about agent access requests. It uses live memory introspection to analyze selected regions of volatile host memory and obtain independent evidence of the system’s operational state. DOCA Argus runs independently of the host, analyzing host memory on BlueField-4 without host-resident agents. This agentless design provides independent runtime visibility while preserving host compute resources. By operating outside the host in its own isolated trust domain, DOCA Argus remains beyond the reach of host software even if the host is compromised. DOCA Argus maps the execution environment in real time—for example, containers to their respective pods and sandboxes to microVMs—and identifies the running processes and their properties within each environment. It also maps relationships between processes and threads, file access, network connections, loaded libraries, CPUs, GPUs, memory, and other system resources. DOCA Argus tracks containers, processes, and loaded libraries using their associated hashes. This runtime context enables NVIDIA Sentry to connect agent access requests to the processes and execution environments behind them, enforcing policies that consider both the requested action and the security and integrity of the agent making it. Using runtime context to evaluate agent access NVIDIA Sentry correlates network connection information from DOCA Tower with runtime context from DOCA Argus to evaluate access requests. NVIDIA Sentry uses this context to enforce policies based on additional attributes and assertions provided by DOCA Argus. It also enriches tamper-evident records of agent activity with runtime context, reducing the need for downstream correlation. Figure 1 shows how these checks work. DOCA Tower uses its policy engine to correlate a network connection with the agent’s process that initiated it, its properties, and the container it belongs to. A network access policy can, for example, require that the container’s hash match a list of approved container hashes. It can also require that the initiating process, identified by its hash, appear in the container software bill of materials (SBOM), have permission to initiate network connections, and use an approved execution path and command-line arguments. DOCA Tower then checks whether policy permits the requested access—for example, access to an API and permission to perform the requested action. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Argus real-time observations and alerts to continuously evaluate agent security.

title: How NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture Secures and Governs AI Agent Workloads at Scale
abstract: Autonomous agents can work for hours on complex tasks, accessing files, tools, the internet, and spawning other agents to collaborate with. Executing complex tasks over long time horizons leads to compounding risk: the agents may download code, build new tools, request additional privileges, and touch more of the underlying infrastructure. The agents’ action paths are determined as they work and reason through the steps needed to complete their goals. As they interact with the tools and systems around them, they adapt their reasoning and behavior to achieve their task. The adaptability of agents is what makes them so powerful, but they are goal-oriented and may not prioritize safety in pursuit of their objectives. In order for agents to work both autonomously and safely, we need to build environments that provide control and visibility in what the agent is doing. An agent cannot govern itself. Security and governance belong in the infrastructure the agent operates in. OpenShell provides deterministic governance outside of the agent’s reach NVIDIA OpenShell is an open-source runtime to build the security and governance needed for agentic systems into the computing infrastructure. OpenShell defines and enforces which systems and data an agent can access, from files and internet services to systems that interact with physical devices. It is the foundation of the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture for building safe AI agents. OpenShell treats agent workloads as untrusted throughout execution. An agent is given access to what it needs, when it needs it. OpenShell has four key components: Gateway: The control plane that manages sandbox lifecycles and policies Supervisor: Checks outbound requests against policy and mediates access to credentials. This runs completely separate to the sandbox Sandbox: Isolates the agent workload and restricts filesystem and process access Policy prover: Adds formal verification, checking whether a policy’s permissions stay within an organization-defined ceiling. As the agents evolve, these components provide the infrastructure controls that allow them to work safely. Extending and integrating OpenShell Extensibility is a core principle of OpenShell’s design. Supervisor middleware lets you inspect, block, or change the content that an agent sends and receives over the network as an additional enforcement layer. Gateway interceptors let operators add deployment-specific governance to OpenShell control-plane operations without modifying the gateway. Organizations also need to establish who an agent acts for, what authority it holds, and whether an action fits the task. Identity, authorization, data protection, and auditing each address part of that problem. OpenShell provides enforcement points where those systems can be integrated. In the reference architecture, OpenShell runs on NVIDIA Vera CPUs. NVIDIA Vera, the compute layer beneath the controls OpenShell defines what agents can do. Vera determines how fast they can do it. Agents operate through loops of dependent steps where each step must complete before the next begins: reasoning, calling tools, executing code, querying data. AI factories run thousands of these loops concurrently, placing new demands on CPU architecture across five dimensions: They need massive core counts to run many concurrent workflows, and fast individual cores to shorten each sequential step. They need high-bandwidth fabric and memory to keep those cores fed with the live data agents depend on. They need massive I/O to move data at speed between CPUs, GPUs, storage, and network. They need hardware-enforced security, because agents increasingly operate on sensitive enterprise data and must be isolated from each other and the host. They need to deliver all of this within the power envelope of a modern data center (more agent work per watt, not just more raw performance). NVIDIA calls this combination the max single-threaded CPU at scale , and NVIDIA Vera is built for it: massive Olympus cores, a second-generation Scalable Coherency Fabric, LPDDR5X memory, Gen 6 I/O, confidential computing, and an energy-efficient design purpose-built for power-limited data centers. Three architectural properties make Vera fast for agent workloads First, 88 NVIDIA-designed Olympus cores with a 10-wide front end, neural branch predictor, and deep out-of-order execution deliver up to 2x performance on critical agentic workloads versus x86, shortening each tool call, code execution, and evaluation. Second, Vera’s second-generation Scalable Coherency Fabric provides up to 3x core-to-core bandwidth and up to 50% lower core-to-core latency than x86 alternatives, keeping data moving predictably under load. Vera also integrates 96 lanes of PCIe Gen 6, delivering the I/O bandwidth to connect GPUs, high-speed storage, and network at the throughput agentic infrastructure demands. Third, up to 1.2 TB/s of LPDDR5X memory bandwidth, with up to 40% lower loaded memory latency than chiplet-based designs, keeps agents supplied with the live context they need without stalling on memory access. LPDDR5X also makes Vera dramatically more efficient: Vera delivers 2x more performance per watt than x86 CPUs, while the LPDDR5X memory subsystem itself draws an order of magnitude less power than competing DDR5-based memory configurations, enabling more agent work within the same power envelope. Agent workloads depend on sandboxes: isolated execution environments where agents run code, invoke tools, and complete tasks without interfering with each other or the host system. The denser and faster those sandboxes spin up, the more agent work a given infrastructure footprint can sustain. CoreWeave , the AI cloud platform purpose-built for training and serving models at scale, found sandbox startup to be more than 3x faster on Vera than on x86, with a single rack supporting more than 11,000 concurrent agent environments. Running Terminal Bench, which measures CPU performance across real agentic loop tasks, CoreWeave found Vera delivered 1.8x faster performance versus x86, across agentic tasks ranging from scripting to database recovery. That density and performance under load is what agent infrastructure actually requires. Figure 1. CoreWeave demonstrates NVIDIA Vera delivers >3x faster sandbox startup and 1.8x faster agentic loop completion versus a leading x86 CPU across 20 real-world agent tasks NVIDIA BlueField and NVIDIA Sentry for hardware-enforced protection OpenShell places authority outside the agent. For deployments that require additional protection, that separation can also extend into purpose-built silicon. NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs provide a hardware-isolated trust domain outside the agent’s reach. In the OpenShell reference architecture, BlueField-4 sits in the I/O path between agents running on Vera and the models they access. NVIDIA Sentry , a security software framework built on NVIDIA DOCA , runs in this independent domain to continuously monitor agent behavior and enforce runtime policy. NVIDIA Sentry observes requests and responses, networking and file activities, verifies identity and delegated authority, and analyzes selected host memory to detect deviations from authorized behavior without relying on agent self-reporting. When it detects a threat or policy violation, BlueField-4 enforces policy in silicon, allowing NVIDIA Sentry to quarantine the agent within milliseconds. Together, they add an optional hardware safeguard alongside OpenShell’s software boundaries. Learn more about NVIDIA Sentry in this technical deep-dive . Bringing secure agent runtimes to scale Running agents in production requires infrastructure that can keep thousands of workflows moving while governing every action they take. Vera provides the compute, memory bandwidth, and I/O to sustain those workflows. OpenShell supplies the runtime boundaries that determine which actions execute and which resources agents can reach.

title: Developing an AI Factory Digital Twin with an Agent-Assisted Workflow
abstract: Building an AI factory digital twin requires developers to bring site plans, equipment assets, and engineering requirements into a consistent model that teams can inspect, revise, and prepare for simulation. Connecting these inputs into an editable workflow helps teams explore design alternatives and incorporate engineering feedback as the design evolves. The NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint , part of NVIDIA DSX Sim , provides reference digital twin assets, sample scripts, and workflows for developing AI factory digital twins. Built on OpenUSD and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries, the blueprint gives developers a foundation for assembling facility and equipment models with SimReady assets, and connecting them with engineering simulation tools. Frontier AI models can help developers work with this foundation through agents and connected applications and tools, as explained in Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations with Frontier AI Agents . Developers guide agents to bring together design inputs, assemble and revise OpenUSD scenes, and inspect the results. The blueprint supplies reusable assets and workflows, and the agents help developers apply and adapt them to specific design requirements (Figure 1). This post demonstrates an agent-assisted workflow for turning reference assets, site data, and design requirements into an editable OpenUSD campus model. Developers can use this approach to explore layouts, revise equipment placement, and prepare designs for engineering review and downstream simulation. Developers connect tools and guide changes, while engineers review results to inform the next iteration. Figure 1. Reference workflow from requirements through an OpenUSD digital twin to an engineering simulation, with results informing the next design revision Providing agents with a design foundation for AI factory modeling Consider a practical question: How should an AI factory hall be configured when the available power is fixed? Changing the compute configuration can impact equipment quantity, placement, electrical distribution, and cooling. Evaluating the alternatives requires those disciplines to work from consistent requirements and design data. An agent needs context before it can make a useful design proposal. Given only photos or renderings, it can produce a model that looks plausible but may have incorrect dimensions and proportions. Reference assets and project documents help ground the proposal, but the resulting model still requires dimensional checks and engineering review. A grounded workflow starts with the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint and reference design, then incorporates the project’s requirements, drawings, equipment information, and site constraints. Each source has a different role: existing geometry supplies reusable buildings and equipment while architectural references inform appearance; aerial imagery and elevation data provide geographic context; project drawings and equipment information establish dimensions and placement; requirements define the conditions the design must satisfy. For example, the team used the NVIDIA Santa Clara Headquarters building, Voyager, as design inspiration for an AI factory campus site based on the DSX reference design. The inputs included: DSX 3D models: Data hall, central utility buildings, substations, generators, cooling equipment, vehicles, and vegetation. Architectural references: Images of Voyager from various aerial and on-the-ground views to inform the roof, facade, solar canopies, and landscaping. Site plans (DSX Reference Design): PDFs describing the campus arrangement and a more detailed first phase, including buildings, roads, utility areas, and access areas. Requirements documents: An indexed collection of architectural drawings, form-factor studies, Basis of Design documents, room layouts, and other records. Geographic data: USGS aerial imagery and elevation data of the selected site used to place the campus in the surrounding terrain. Figure 2. The supplied inputs resulted in an editable campus site model combining the DSX Blueprint reference design with an architectural facade inspired by Voyager Together, these sources provide a starting point for an agent-assisted workflow and basis for reviewing its output. They help teams trace design choices to their sources—for example, building placement to a site plan and facade styling to an architectural reference. That traceability supports review; dimensional accuracy still depends on checking the model against the applicable drawings, specifications, and site constraints. Building an OpenUSD campus site model using an AI agent To implement this workflow, a frontier AI model runs in an agent harness: software that manages context, instructions, and tool calls. Skills encode repeatable tasks and AI factory domain knowledge. Developers connect modeling and analysis operations through tool interfaces, including the Model Context Protocol (MCP), where supported, and define which changes the agent may propose or apply. In the campus model example, existing DSX reference designed buildings from the DSX Blueprint and equipment supplied the starting geometry, while the site plans guided placement and first-phase details. The team supplied photographs and the architectural references from the NVIDIA Voyager campus to guide the architectural additions. For the solar canopy, the frontier AI agent used USD Content Agents to help generate its geometry and materials, then refined the design using the Voyager references. This gave the team an editable architectural element to review alongside the existing buildings and equipment. The canopy remained a conceptual design where an engineering team could check for dimensions, structural properties, and suitability for simulation. The team then combined the reused assets and new architectural geometry in additive USD layers, keeping changes separate from the source assets. In the Omniverse RTX viewport, the team could inspect the canopy in the context of the campus, review its appearance and placement, and revise the model as design decisions change. USGS aerial data was used for the landscape and elevation plan. Figure 3. The campus model is fully realized in an Omniverse RTX viewport, taking design layout and existing assets from DSX Blueprint and elements from real images of Voyager for the site design Extending the campus model to evaluate a fixed power budget The campus model could support a subsequent capacity planning study: How should an AI factory hall be configured within a fixed power budget? The proposed extension would connect the modeled layout with compute, electrical, and cooling requirements to evaluate alternative configurations. One starting point is an illustrative NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 inference comparison. It contrasts a baseline using MaxP —the highest static GPU-level power setting—with DSX MaxLPS , an AI factory design and operating framework that coordinates facility design, dynamic power allocation, and performance-per-watt optimization. Applying this comparison to a hall would require evaluating the support power, cooling, and networking infrastructure. Normalized to a 1 MW power basis, assuming a power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.1, the illustrative scenario shows a DSX MaxLPS capacity of 400 GPUs and aggregate token throughput of 1.35x the MaxP baseline (Figure 4). These figures are reference assumptions for the proposed study, not results generated by the campus model. Figure 4. Illustrative NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 inference comparison, normalized to a 1 MW power basis with PUE 1.1. The comparison provides context for the proposed capacity-planning workflow; it does not represent results from the campus model or specify a deployable rack layout.

title: Achieve Productive AI Capacity Faster and More Predictably with NVIDIA DSX POD
abstract: AI factories turn energy into intelligence. But before an AI workload can produce its first token, operators must bring an interconnected system of compute, networking, storage, power, cooling, and software online as one productive unit. In a conventional data center build, teams must first select the site, design power and cooling for the deployment, lay out the data center, and plan and install racks and cables. Then they can validate the network and cluster incrementally and bring service online. This work requires coordinated specialized labor, with critical dependencies among installation, infrastructure readiness, and system testing. Delays can push back bring-up and the date the infrastructure begins producing tokens. NVIDIA DSX POD shifts more of this work into a controlled factory environment. One of multiple AI factory implementation models supported by NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform , NVIDIA DSX POD reference design is the standardized, factory-built implementation. It enables partners to build standardized containers that pre-integrate AI infrastructure, complete critical validation before shipment, and connect to prepared site infrastructure after delivery. The result is a repeatable approach designed to reduce onsite integration complexity and help operators reach productive AI capacity faster and more predictably. This post explains the foundation of NVIDIA DSX POD, how the reference design aligns with the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform , and how NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners work through product engineering, deployment, and support. A design foundation for moving AI factory integration upstream Modular and prefabricated data centers already exist. The engineering challenge for an AI factory extends beyond placing conventional IT equipment in an enclosure. Rack-scale AI systems combine high-density compute, high-speed scale-up and scale-out networking, liquid cooling, power delivery, telemetry, and management software. These elements behave as one system. Their mechanical, electrical, thermal, and network requirements must remain within specification during factory integration, transportation, installation, and operation. NVIDIA DSX POD provides the design foundation for partners to install rack-scale systems in containers at the factory, functionally test the integrated unit, transport it, and bring it online safely through repeatable processes at the destination. NVIDIA’s investment spans the engineering disciplines required to make that possible, including rack layout, structural loading, power, cooling, cabling, service access, reliability, and validation. This work extends the progression toward greater factory integration to reduce installation complexity and accelerate deployment. NVIDIA has moved from chips and boards to complete rack-scale systems, and large-scale reference architectures like NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD . NVIDIA DSX POD carries this approach into a factory-built AI factory implementation, moving most component integration from the customer site into a controlled manufacturing environment. The reference design does not make containerization mandatory for every AI factory. Conventional data center construction and onsite-integrated designs remain important options. NVIDIA DSX POD adds a standardized path for large-scale deployments where schedule predictability, repeatability, and reduced onsite work are priorities. Architecture aligned with NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform NVIDIA DSX is the broad design framework for co-designed AI infrastructure. It brings compute, networking, storage, power, cooling, facility controls, and software together at the data center level. Customers and partners can implement that framework in different physical forms. NVIDIA DSX POD is a specific realization of that broader design: a standardized AI factory architecture composed of factory-built container types and defined interfaces between them. The architecture is designed around the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform and its rack-scale systems. The reference design describes a complete AI factory rather than a compute enclosure in isolation. It accounts for compute, service and management functions, scale-out networking, storage, power, cooling, cabling, and other supporting infrastructure. Technical requirements for factory-integrated deployment The central purpose of the NVIDIA DSX POD reference design is to make the full deployment process repeatable. That requires coordinated requirements across the following areas: compute integration, networking and storage, cabling and controls, power delivery, liquid cooling, and mechanical design and transportation. Compute integration The NVIDIA DSX POD compute container is designed for NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack scale infrastructure. The design defines how compute and supporting racks fit within the enclosure and how partners address structural support, weight distribution, equipment restraint, service clearances, airflow and liquid-cooling access, rack-level power, and network connectivity. Factory integration also changes the validation boundary. Instead of treating each rack as an independent shipment that will be assembled into a cluster onsite, partners validate the installed compute environment as a deployment unit. The validation plan can cover rack inventory, firmware and configuration baselines, power-on checks, fabric connectivity, sensor operation, cooling integrity, and system-level functional tests before the container leaves the factory. Networking and storage AI workloads depend on predictable movement of model data, training data, checkpoint data, and inference context across the AI factory. The reference design therefore treats networking and storage as part of the system architecture rather than as site-specific additions made after compute arrives. The design defines the connectivity required within a compute container, between containers, and from the modular system to the customer’s external network. It accounts for scale-out fabrics, service and management networks, fiber entry points, trunk cabling, cable routing, labeling, bend radius, service access, and validation of factory-installed link before shipment. Storage requirements follow the same principle. The architecture defines the required capacity, performance, connectivity, management, and service characteristics while allowing the final equipment implementation to reflect the deployment scale and partner solution. This enables storage and networking to arrive as coordinated parts of the AI factory instead of independent systems that must be reconciled late in site integration. Cabling and controls NVIDIA DSX POD reduces the onsite work of cabling in a rack-scale deployment, moving rack-to-rack network cabling, power wiring, control wiring, and sensor integration into the factory wherever practical. The reference design clearly defines cable paths, separation requirements, termination points, labeling conventions, test procedures, and serviceability requirements to help partners easily install and test these connections under controlled conditions to reduce the number of field terminations required after delivery. Power delivery DSX POD makes power delivery seamless with a standard input 800 VDC power design that begins with the electrical input to the core containers and continues through protection, distribution, grounding, rack connections, controls, and telemetry. The reference design defines the power characteristics and interfaces required by the installed AI infrastructure. Partners then engineer the upstream generation, conversion, and regional electrical solution for the customer site. This separation is important because utility conditions, codes, equipment availability, and grid architectures differ across regions. A common interface at the container boundary enables repeatable core designs while preserving flexibility in how ecosystem partners deliver power to each deployment.

title: Train Qwen3 on AWS Trainium with torchtitan
abstract: Using torchtitan on AWS Trainium means using it the way you always have. TorchNeuron registers Trainium as a native PyTorch device, which lets torchtitan use it through standard PyTorch interfaces. You can use these configurations to pre-train from random initialization or fine-tune published weights. You can also customize the model implementation and kernels for your workload. In this post, you train Qwen3 three ways on a single trn2.48xlarge . The first method uses Transformers v5 as a modeling backend in torchtitan. It runs Hub models through AutoModelForCausalLM and reads and writes published safetensors directly. The second method switches to torchtitan’s native Qwen3 by changing config.model_spec . The third adds Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) mixture-of-experts (MoE) kernels from the torchtitan-neuron recipes and then uses torchtitan’s override registry to attach your own kernel. All three configurations use the same torchrun launch pattern and config structure. To follow this walkthrough, use a single trn2.48xlarge with either the AWS Deep Learning AMI for Neuron or a Neuron PyTorch training container. Both environments provide the Neuron driver, runtime, and compiler required to train on Trainium. Before you install torchtitan-neuron , check whether your environment already includes it. The following command prints the installed version and package path: This walkthrough uses the versions in the following table. To reproduce the examples, pin these versions. The Transformers v5 integration and Trainium-specific override modules can change between torchtitan releases. When torch_neuronx is installed, TorchNeuron registers Trainium as the neuron device and torchtitan detects it at startup. In eager mode, Neuron compiles operations as they execute. With torch.compile , Neuron compiles the captured graph. This same launch pattern works across all three configurations. For the versions used in this walkthrough, install torchtitan-neuron and torchtitan’s remaining dependencies with --no-deps to preserve the Neuron build of torch: Before you start training, get the Qwen3 model artifacts from Hugging Face Hub. Store them in a local directory that you can pass to the training config: Each training configuration is a Python config function. The three examples start from a base config that you update for each step. In the first configuration, Transformers v5 builds Qwen3 through AutoModelForCausalLM . The Hub model definition supplies the implementation used for the forward and backward passes. You select the model by setting its Hub ID in the config. Start with transformers_modeling_backend_full() . It leaves the fields that map to Hugging Face configuration keys unset, so AutoConfig.from_pretrained() loads the model architecture from the Hub. Create neuron_qwen3.py in the torchtitan-neuron repository root, where you run the training command. Add the imports, model artifact path, and base config: This command launches 64 training processes, one for each logical NeuronCore. --module neuron_qwen3 imports the local config module. --config v5_qwen3_4b selects the configuration function. The data parallel setting shards the model across all 64 ranks. To fine-tune from published weights, enable checkpoint loading and point initial_load_path to ASSETS . The state-dictionary adapter adjusts the leading model. prefix and handles tied embeddings. It saves the final checkpoint as Hugging Face safetensors. Use the first training-step loss as a quick check that torchtitan loaded the published weights. For Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 , the verified run produced a step 1 loss of 6.54 from published weights and 12.43 from random initialization. After training, load the exported checkpoint with AutoModelForCausalLM and load_state_dict . A successful round trip reports no missing or unexpected keys other than lm_head.weight , which Qwen3-4B ties to the token embeddings. This confirms that the files remain a standard Hugging Face checkpoint. Figure 1: The published checkpoint starts with a loss of 6.54, and the exported weights load without missing or unexpected keys In the second configuration, torchtitan builds its native Qwen3Model . Add the native Qwen3 imports and config function to neuron_qwen3.py : This example starts from qwen3_32b() because the tested torchtitan build does not provide a generic qwen3_4b() config builder. The next line replaces the 32B model specification with the 4B specification. The remaining fields reproduce the tested run. config.model_spec selects the model class and defines how torchtitan shards the model and maps its checkpoint keys. Here, model_registry("4B", attn_backend="sdpa") selects torchtitan’s native Qwen3 implementation with scaled dot product attention (SDPA). In the third configuration, torchtitan runs mixture-of-experts layers with kernels written in NKI, the Neuron kernel language. Add the required imports and Qwen3 MoE config function to neuron_qwen3.py : This configuration uses data parallel sharding across 64 ranks with a tensor parallel degree of 1. It does not use expert parallelism. num_experts=64 sets the number of experts in the model, not the expert parallel degree. Setting CompileConfig(enable=False) runs this example in eager mode. TorchNeuron supports registered NKI operators in both eager execution and torch.compile . In the torchtitan build used for this walkthrough, qwen3_nki_moe_config() replaces the MoE block with the NKI grouped-experts implementation. It also selects SDPA and the gather-free rotary embedding. When you enable torch.compile , add "grad_clip" to CompileConfig.components to compile gradient-norm clipping. NKI kernels enter training as PyTorch operators. wrap_nki makes an NKI kernel callable from PyTorch, and nki_op registers the operator. register_autograd attaches its backward pass using routing metadata saved during the forward pass. The example reduces Qwen3-30B-A3B to 4 layers and 64 experts so it fits on one trn2.48xlarge . It routes each token to 4 experts with top_k=4 . In some cases, you might want to optimize an operation for the tensor shapes in your model. A specialized kernel can tailor its tiling and data movement to those shapes. It can also replace a performance-critical sequence of PyTorch operations with one optimized operator. You can write the kernel yourself or start with one from nkilib . This example uses rope_hf from nkilib.core.embeddings , which expects the Hugging Face tensor layout and supports its own backward mode. This example demonstrates kernel registration and autograd integration, not a performance improvement. Create my_neuron_kernels.py in the repository root, where you launch training. torchtitan stores query and key as [batch, seq, heads, head_dim] , whereas rope_hf expects [batch, heads, seq, head_dim] . Convert the layout inside the operator and allocate the output tensors with torch.empty_like() : rope_hf computes gradients when you call it with backward=True . Register a second operator for that mode. Save the rotary cache during the forward pass so the backward pass can reuse it. Return None for the cache gradient because the cache is not differentiable. Because rope_hf requires a supported sequence length, validate that constraint before calling the kernel. Subclass CosSinRoPE and call rope_fwd from apply_rotary_emb : Register NKIRoPE as the replacement for CosSinRoPE . derive() copies the shared configuration fields into the replacement config: To load the custom override, pass its module name to --override.imports . torchtitan imports the registry entry before it builds the model: Before training starts, torchtitan logs each config node that the override replaces. Confirm that the output contains one nki_rope entry for each Qwen3 layer: Set the sequence length to a multiple of 128 * LNC , which is 256 when LNC is 2. Reshape the rotary cache to [seq, head_dim * 2] , with cosine values in the first half and sine values in the second.

title: How U.S. Hunger connects leaders and data using Amazon Quick
abstract: For U.S. Hunger, feeding families takes more than delivering food to them. It takes understanding the people behind each request, the pressures they face, and the business that makes the mission possible. That means connecting information across the organization. Its mission is to feed families today and unite them to a healthier tomorrow. U.S. Hunger reports delivering more than 250 million meals. Its work has reached 59 countries historically and is now concentrated primarily in the United States. The organization reports approximately 500 percent growth over four years, compared with only 15–20 percent headcount growth. For a lean team at that scale, every hour and every decision matters. With Amazon Quick , U.S. Hunger can explore organizational data directly, colleagues can work from shared definitions, and leaders can examine financial information alongside the circumstances families report. U.S. Hunger’s experience shows how those capabilities fit into the daily work of a lean nonprofit. Rick Whitted spent 30 years in banking before making the leap to lead U.S. Hunger. His connection to food insecurity, however, began long before that career change. When Rick and his wife were in their mid-twenties, he left his career to start a business. They lost everything. Even though he went to work every day, they relied on help from family to get by. He remembers coming home to find a pantry box on the table, left by aunts or grandparents. Seeing that box broke him. More than 20 years later, when the board chair asked him to consider leading U.S. Hunger, his wife reminded him of those days, when their own family needed help putting food on the table. To her, leading U.S. Hunger was a chance to help families going through what they had experienced themselves. Rick cried, called the chair back, and accepted. “The families we serve today, their stories are my story.” — Rick Whitted, President and CEO, U.S. Hunger More than six years into the role, that personal connection remains at the heart of Rick’s leadership. U.S. Hunger first learned about Quick through an AWS Social Entrepreneur Accelerator event led by Kat Esser. Rick saw an opportunity to explore the organization’s data directly, following questions as they arose without asking the technology team for a new data pull each time. Chief technology officer (CTO) Ezekiel Brooks helped make that possible by giving Rick access to core datasets from Full Cart, U.S. Hunger’s food-assistance program. Full Cart delivers donor-funded food directly to households in need. Quick gave Rick room to explore the information at his own pace and ask follow-up questions. The organization’s data became his sandbox. The data comes from Impact Manager, U.S. Hunger’s proprietary cloud-based data platform supporting its food-assistance work. Quick pulls data from SQL Server into its in-memory engine, SPICE , through scheduled refresh jobs at 2 AM ET each night. The technology team and a colleague working with research data prepare the datasets and provide definitions to help Rick interpret the information. Figure 1: U.S. Hunger refreshes SQL Server data into SPICE at 2 AM ET each night for analysis in Amazon Quick Direct exploration was the starting point, but the moment when everything clicked came with a different discovery: Quick Spaces . For Rick, Spaces changed the role Quick could play in the organization. A Space gives colleagues a shared place to work with documents, definitions, and analyses relevant to a particular area of the business. That matters when leaders need to understand one another’s work and make decisions together. Shared definitions of key performance indicators (KPIs) help them agree on what a measure means. Financial documents and planning tools provide context for discussions about the organization’s resources. Rick sees this as his a-ha moment: using Quick to help the leadership team run the organization together. “Quick provides a live connection to how leadership thinks through problems. I can pick up where our CEO left off in a financial model or see how he’s framing a KPI, without scheduling another meeting.” — Sarah Aranguibel, Chief of Staff, U.S. Hunger The leadership team brings together a shared document of KPIs, developed over more than a year while working across NetSuite, Salesforce, Impact Manager, and its payroll system. The document records definitions, where measures come from, and goals. Rick also uses Quick to develop definitions for client tiers and shares them in the same Space. “With all the knowledge and data we have, Space reduces as much noise as possible and narrows my discussion.” — Rick Whitted, President and CEO, U.S. Hunger Selecting the Space relevant to a question keeps the conversation focused on the right documents. The financial Space is shared with the CTO, chief operating officer (COO), and finance leadership, giving colleagues access to the tools and business context behind an analysis. Together, these materials show colleagues what the organization measures and the business logic behind it. U.S. Hunger has given 17 colleagues access to Quick across its executive leadership, technology team, Full Cart program, Finance, Compliance, and supporting functions. For its CEO, chat is the primary day-to-day artificial intelligence (AI) workspace, and Spaces is the capability he uses most. Using a Space containing Salesforce call reports, Rick is drafting instructions for the technology team: which measures to include, where the data comes from, and what each measure means. In Quick, he can comment directly on the generated draft and regenerate it with multiple changes incorporated. He can review and refine the instructions alongside the source reports, without spending time moving documents and comments between Word and chat. After completion, the instructions will guide reporting improvements for the member-engagement team, helping the program’s operational leaders and COO monitor the team’s work. U.S. Hunger uses Amazon Quick Research to investigate current events, inform communications, and connect policy questions with its survey data. The CEO is also exploring how that data could serve a wider audience. With the version history in Quick Research, he can revisit earlier versions as he refines an investigation. Understanding food insecurity requires information about who is struggling and the circumstances behind that struggle. In September 2025, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) announced that it would end future Household Food Security Reports. With that longstanding reporting series ending, access to other sources of evidence becomes especially important. U.S. Hunger wants to make the information it collects available beyond its own organization. It envisions a national hunger-data resource where researchers and the public can explore the experiences of families seeking assistance. Alongside that access, the organization plans an enterprise offering that companies can purchase, helping fund its mission. As Rick puts it, the goal is for “ the very data we’re using to help people ” to become “ the flywheel that feeds the very people we’re trying to help .” The national dashboard brings food insecurity together with income, education, health, and social needs. Filters help leaders examine different populations and use those findings in conversations with prospective partners about why families need help. For financial planning, Rick uses a Space containing audits, cash-flow information, and board budget views. A debt-service calculator and nonprofit financial-health worksheet help him share his banking experience with the COO. The financial documents provide context for drafting audit footnotes. With over a decade of financial documents available in the Space, Rick can ask Quick to compare patterns over time and explore questions about current operations.

title: Beyond the KV cache: Training and serving i14’s Laplace 3B linear attention model on AWS Trainium2 with native PyTorch
abstract: Most large language models (LLMs) use transformer architectures with softmax attention. During inference, their key-value (KV) cache grows with the conversation or document context. This can reduce concurrency, increase serving cost, and force agentic applications to discard useful history. i14 designed Laplace 3B as a linear attention alternative. Its recurrent state stays at 29.5 MB per sequence, independent of context length. Working with AWS, i14 used native PyTorch support through TorchNeuron Native to bring this custom architecture to AWS Trainium2 . This preserved its Gated Linear Attention (GLA) design and Muon optimizer. On one trn2.48xlarge instance, Laplace 3B trained at about 120,000 tokens per second. The model served 11,544 output tokens per second across 1,280 concurrent sequences. This post explains the model design, the changes i14 made for Trainium2, and the training and inference results. i14 is an AI research and technology company that develops model architectures, components, and runtimes. Its work draws on AI, computational cognitive science, and research into how biological systems learn over time. i14 applies these ideas to models that can retain long-range context without allowing serving state to grow with every token. Transformer softmax attention compares tokens across the context. During training, this computation grows quadratically with sequence length. During inference, the KV cache grows as the model processes more tokens. Linear attention reorganizes the computation around a recurrent state that is updated for each token. Laplace 3B uses GLA to compress prior context into a fixed-size matrix state. This changes training attention from O( T 2) to O( T ) and keeps inference state fixed at 29.5 MB per sequence. Linear attention compresses history rather than retaining every key and value. You must therefore evaluate retrieval quality for your workloads. The fixed state can benefit long-running agents, large-document analysis, and applications that need persistent memory with predictable serving requirements. The original implementation of Laplace 3B used GPU-optimized Triton kernels. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center (GenAIIC) team first rewrote the GLA kernel with standard PyTorch operators for Trainium2. After comparing both approaches, the team chose the beta version of TorchNeuron Native, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium , because it performed better. The implementation required three changes: The engineering challenges section describes each change in detail. AWS Trainium is a family of AWS machine learning (ML) accelerators designed for model training and inference. A trn2.48xlarge instance combines 16 Trainium2 chips, 64 logical NeuronCores, high-bandwidth memory, and NeuronLink-v3 connectivity. These resources support the distributed training and inference configurations described in this post. Three properties of Trainium2 shaped the implementation: software-managed on-chip memory (Challenge 1), a fast chip-to-chip interconnect (Challenge 2), and a static compiler (Challenge 3). The compiler traces the GLA recurrence as a fixed graph. Software-managed on-chip memory. Each NeuronCore has a 28 MiB State Buffer (SBUF) with 128 partitions and a 2 MiB partial-sum buffer (PSUM). The PSUM is wired to a 128×128 systolic Tensor Engine, alongside separate vector and scalar units. The SBUF is not a cache: the compiler schedules every HBM-to-SBUF transfer ahead of time, so the data is in place with no evictions or misses (Figure 1). Figure 1: NeuronCore-v3 internal architecture. Software-managed SBUF (28 MiB, 128 partitions), Tensor Engine (128×128 systolic array), Vector Engine, Scalar Engine, and GPSIMD cores. Laplace 3B is the 24-layer i14 decoder, where every layer replaces softmax attention with Simple GLA. Figure 2 follows one layer from the input x t at the top to the output x t + 1 at the bottom. This section explains each module: normalization and convolution, the QKVG projection, the GLA mixer, and the feed-forward channel mixer. Normalization and convolution. Each token’s residual-stream vector x t ∈ ℝ D ( D = 3, 072 ) passes through a LayerNorm and a depth-wise causal Conv1d of width k = 4 with SiLU. This gives every position a 4-gram summary before the mixer. The GLA mixer then does content-based retrieval over the whole history through its decaying state. QKVG projection. The post-conv output goes through one fused matrix W q k v g ∈ ℝ 9, 216 × 3, 072 , where 9, 216 = H × (2 d k + 2 d v ) . It splits into four per-token streams: queries q t , keys k t , values v t , and a gate g t ( H = 16 , d k = 96 , d v = 192 ). The gate is used after the mixer. Figure 2: Laplace decoder layer architecture. Green = fixed (no params), gray = learned, yellow = recurrent state, blue = projection. GLA mixer. Each head h keeps a matrix state S t ( h ) of size d k × d v (96 × 192), a compressed, decaying record of past key-value pairs. At each token, it updates as: GLA recurrent-state update equation GLA self-augmentation equation Decay schedule. The per-head decay rate λ h controls how fast a head forgets past tokens. It is fixed at initialization (not learned) and set by a geometric schedule. The schedule gives the 16 heads a spread of memory lengths and defines each head’s log-decay rate γ h : Channel mixer (FFN). After the attention block and its residual, a second LayerNorm feeds a GLU (SiLU) FFN with inner dimension 8,192. Its three matrices are two up-projections W 1 , W 2 ∈ ℝ 8, 192 × D and one down-projection W 3 ∈ ℝ D × 8, 192 . A second residual follows. The state S ( h ) is fixed at d k × d v = 96 × 192 per head regardless of sequence length. As a result, inference is O (1) per token, and training is O ( T ) rather than O ( T 2 ) . Each of the three changes raised its own engineering challenge. On GPU, GLA runs as the fused Triton kernel fused_chunk_simple_gla from the flash-linear-attention library. The GenAIIC team re-expressed it with standard PyTorch operators running through TorchNeuron Native , as explicit loops over fixed-size chunks. The chunk count is fixed at compile time and sets the backward-unroll depth. The team uses fla_num_chunks = 16, so each chunk holds C = 128 tokens. Within each chunk c , the intra-chunk output is masked linear attention, and the running state S adds earlier context: Chunked GLA intra-chunk output The state then advances to the next chunk: Here λ C is the per-head decay compounded over the chunk. The 16 intra-chunk computations run in parallel, and only the state update is sequential (Figure 3). Figure 3: GLA chunked recurrence with parallel intra-chunk attention and a sequential state chain. Because the SBUF has 128 partitions, each 128-token chunk maps one token per partition, with no padding or cross-partition movement. This alignment increased measured throughput by 14 percent (Figure 4). Figure 4: Chunk size C = 128 maps one-to-one onto the 128 SBUF partitions. Muon orthogonalizes each gradient before the update. For each of the 96 two-dimensional weight matrices (2.718 billion parameters), it runs five Newton–Schulz iterations (Algorithm 1). The distributed problem. The Gram matrix A = X X ⊤ correlates every row of the weight with every other row. Under Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP2), each of the 64 ranks holds only 1/64 of the rows. A shard-local X X ⊤ therefore yields only a diagonal block and drops every cross-shard term (Figure 5). Figure 5: Newton–Schulz under FSDP2: the shard-local Gram block, and gather/broadcast compared with all_to_all. Naive approach: Gather and broadcast. Every rank gathers the full gradient (5.44 GB), one rank runs Newton–Schulz, and it broadcasts the result. This moves 10.87 GB per step while the other 63 ranks wait. Production approach: all_to_all transposition. In MuonFSDP2, one all_to_all gives each rank a few complete matrices, all 64 ranks run Newton–Schulz in parallel, and a second all_to_all returns the results.

title: 飛書豆包工作AI先鋒未來人才大賽：企業正在爭搶會用AI做成事的人
abstract: 飛書豆包工作AI先鋒未來人才大賽：企業正在爭搶會用AI做成事的人 量子位的朋友們 2026-10-21 10:37:39 來源： 量子位 先看真實問題解決力 10月20日，飛書豆包工作AI先鋒未來人才大賽總決賽在北京舉行。12組選手圍繞企業真實業務問題展開角逐，使用飛書與豆包工作完成調研、協作和成果交付，接受企業家、業務負責人及高校學者的現場檢驗。 飛書CEO謝欣，元氣森林創始人唐彬森，華熙生物董事長兼CEO趙燕，珀萊雅股份總經理侯亞孟，小米集團人力資源副總裁王棟，高途集團聯合創始人羅斌，安克創新CIO龔銀，影石研究院負責人兼CAIO亓魯，斯坦福大學人工智慧、機器人與未來教育中心主任蔣裡，清華大學經濟管理學院領導力與組織管理系教授、系主任李寧，復旦大學國際關係與公共事務學院副教授、全球人工智慧創新治理中心副主任蔣昌建等嘉賓出席活動。 飛書CEO 謝欣 談及辦賽初衷，謝欣表示，飛書一端連線著學生嚮往的先進企業，瞭解企業對AI人才的需求；另一端也看到，大學生面對AI時代的職業選擇仍有不確定性。大賽希望彌合這種人才錯位，讓學生與企業在真實業務中相遇。企業需要的不是會用AI寫PPT的人，而是能用AI解決真實問題、交付成果的人；作品則讓企業看見學生的潛力，並判斷他們未來將如何工作。 活動現場，飛書和豆包工作與數智教育發展國際大學聯盟共同釋出《AI時代人才標準全景觀察》，彙集4300多支戰隊資料和108家企業人才觀。謝欣表示，希望讓更多年輕人有機會解決真實業務問題，也讓真正能把事情做成的人更早被企業看見——“未來AI人才，先看AI先鋒。” 從企業真題到業務成果，作品成為新的能力證明 經過現場路演、評委追問和綜合評審，“秋陽裡Pipeline”獲得金獎，“見微智探”“氨心排程”獲得銀獎，“XwX”“安燈常綠隊”“最喜歡vibe coding啦”獲得銅獎。 比名次更值得關注的，是企業為什麼願意把機會給一個學生。學歷和專業背景仍是參考，但企業越來越看重學生能否理解真實業務、正確使用AI，並把想法變成可驗證的成果。侯亞孟表示，企業需要的未來人才，不只是會使用AI工具，更要能把知識轉化為業務應用、推動AI在真實場景中落地，駕馭AI，而不是被AI牽著走。 在雲圖控股專案中，張青青使用飛書和豆包工作打造生產排程數字員工“氨心”，將產供銷資訊轉化為排程決策。趙燕表示，企業需要的AI人才，不僅要能深入產業、解決真實問題，還要懂得界定物理、商業和安全邊界；不是隻用AI生成方案，而是要理解採購、生產、裝置執行等業務，在守住邊界的同時推動AI落地。 面對山海星辰“一人劇組、爆款出海”的命題，邱楊、李淑潔、楊浩用豆包工作搭建AI內容生產流水線。傳統真人短劇需要25至40天、成本50萬至100萬元，團隊最快3天、3000元即可完成一部120分鐘短劇。 在睿創微納“見微智探”專案中，選手鄭一凡、張一帆提出，“雷達負責看見，AI負責看懂，人只需要在關鍵時刻做決策。”團隊使用飛書和豆包工作搭建全過程處置工作流，讓雷達識別結果真正進入業務決策。 評價果卡科技“果然智鏈”專案時，唐彬森表示，企業需要的AI人才，不是用AI寫PPT，而是能深入供應鏈，把水下的業務規則變成可執行方案，真正減少浪費、提升效率，並最終體現在財務報表上。 AI時代，專業不再是能力的邊界。擁有復旦大學歷史學本碩背景的孫夢，為長隆集團設計了一款AI旅伴產品。她表示，歷史學與AI產品設計看似相距甚遠，但都需要發現問題、推導問題和解決問題，“這或許正是通識教育的意義”。 數十家企業帶著崗位來到現場，大賽變成“mini秋招會” 總決賽最精彩的環節，是學生反選Offer。“安燈常綠隊”、“最喜歡vibe coding啦”和“秋陽裡Pipeline”進入反選環節。企業帶著真實崗位和發展機會走到選手面前，三支戰隊則根據崗位方向、成長空間和業務興趣作出選擇，現場有多家企業給到全職offer選擇。這一環節讓企業與人才從單向篩選走向雙向選擇：企業通過作品識別人，學生通過真實業務認識企業。 企業招人開放麥環節 當天上午，數十家企業參與“企業招人開放麥”。華熙生物、山海星辰、珀萊雅等企業的校招負責人帶著崗位現場宣講，學生圍繞崗位要求、AI能力和成長路徑頻頻提問。大賽由此成為學生與企業直接對話、獲得職業機會的“mini秋招會”。 本屆大賽向選手開放全部飛書AI功能並提供無限Token權益，其中80%以上的Token使用發生在豆包工作。對學生而言，豆包工作幫助他們把知識變成作品、把能力變成機會；對企業而言，大賽提供了一種比簡歷篩選更接近真實工作的識人方式。 大賽傳遞出一個清晰判斷：未來人才，是能夠與AI協作，把真實問題做成結果的人。會用豆包工作，不只是掌握一項工具，更意味著能夠理解業務、組織協作、駕馭AI並對結果負責。AI能力，正在成為大學生髮展競爭力的新標配。 本文由飛書豆包工作提供，量子位獲授權轉載，觀點歸原作者所有。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 AI先鋒未來人才大賽 豆包工作 飛書 量子位的朋友們 title: 理想宣佈：電池自燃報廢賠新車！自研6年後有底氣了
abstract: 理想宣佈：電池自燃報廢賠新車！自研6年後有底氣了 傑西卡 2026-10-21 09:04:35 來源： 量子位 電池、電驅、超充一把梭，冬天多跑30公里 傑西卡 發自 ROBO-車 量子位ROBO | 公眾號 AI4ROBO “理想必須要成為一家最懂電池的智慧電動企業。” 被問到為什麼要花精力去自研電池時，李想給出了他的判斷。 緊接著 Power Day電動技術釋出會 上，理想正式釋出 連山電動技術體系 ，集中披露其在 電池、電機、電控、碳化矽功率晶片以及超充網路 方面的研發成果。 5C磷酸鐵鋰電芯 ，能量密度比2C電芯反而更高；冬季電池峰值功率提升 40% 以上；自研碳化矽功率晶片累計裝車400萬顆，理想稱至今保持零失效紀錄。 理想還首次公佈了 電池自燃、碰撞起火 相關的終身保障政策： 對於符合條件的電池質量問題引發自燃，以及碰撞、底部刮蹭導致的電池起火，理想將根據車輛損失情況提供相應賠付。比如自研電池因質量問題自燃，整車達到報廢標準， 理想將賠一輛同配置新車 。 信心並不是一蹴而就。李想在幾天前透露，自研電池是在6年前的 2020年 就定好的事。 有意思的是，連續兩天發微博的李想，到了正式釋出會卻全程坐在臺下，或沉思，或微笑。 開場的是理想聯合創始人、總裁兼總工程師 馬東輝 ，同時登臺的還有理想電池、電驅、充電網路的三位技術負責人。 他們講了大量材料、演算法、晶片和製造工藝的細節，也給出了理想堅持六年自研的理由。 理想連山釋出，電池、電驅和超充全面升級 理想在Power Day展示的技術成果，主要集中在三方面： 提高電池的充電效率、續航和壽命，進一步降低電驅能耗，以及擴大超充網路覆蓋、改善補能體驗。 此次釋出的連山，包含 連山電池、連山電驅、超充裝置及自建超充網路 ，背後還有一套連山質量預警平臺，負責連線核心零部件的製造、檢測和車輛使用資料。 連山電池：430公里增程，780公里純電 此次釋出會公佈，新一代增程L8將搭載理想自研5C三元鋰電池，CLTC純電續航達到 430公里 ；即將於10月28日上市的2026款理想i6，CLTC續航最高達到 780公里 ，相比2025款提升8%。 續航提升之外，理想更強調一個技術結果： 在實現5C超充的同時，電池能量密度沒有因此降低 。 理想此次公佈了兩項正負極改進： 負極 採用梯度孔隙電極技術，外部大孔隙提高鋰離子傳輸效率、內部高密度保證儲能； 正極 通過不同尺寸顆粒復配，提高活性材料填充密度。新一代磷酸鐵鋰5C電芯相比2C電芯，能量密度提升 2.6% 。 電池包也經過重新設計：取消長縱梁改用新框架結構，將冷卻管路與碰撞梁整合，並最佳化配電單元和上蓋匹配，合計額外增加約 7.4度電 的佈置空間。 硬體之外，軟體演算法也迎來升級。 磷酸鐵鋰電池電壓平臺平坦，電量估算一直是難點。理想開發了 ATR自適應軌跡庫重構演算法 ，結合歷史充放電資料和動態電壓修正，將電量估算誤差控制在 3%以內 。 冬季方面， APC功率自適應演算法 在不改變電池硬體的情況下將冬季峰值功率提高40%以上；電池餘熱再利用於座艙供暖，多項最佳化疊加後，官方稱冬季等效續航可增加 30公里 。 硬體不變，車輛的續航和低溫效能仍有繼續最佳化的空間，這正是整車軟體控制與電池技術協同帶來的變化。 電池安全及終身質保 理想此次為連山電池公佈了六道安全防線： 防磕碰、防進水、防漏液、防熱擴散、製造質量管控和執行風險預警 。 針對日常託底、碰撞等情況，理想在電池包底部設定多層防護結構，並最佳化電芯的抗壓能力。 在理想展示的等效500焦耳底部衝擊測試中，連山電池未發生起火、爆炸，防水效能達到IPX8、IPX9K等級。 熱擴散防護則通過電芯隔熱材料、定向排氣以及應急水冷實現，降低熱失控向周邊擴散的風險。按照官方測試結果，50℃環境下單顆電芯熱失效，電池包可實現 24小時不起火 。 電池壽命方面，新一代三元電池採用 雙極速冷架構 ，換熱效率提高30%、電芯間溫差控制在5℃以內。 理想稱，2026年搭載自研5C超充電池的增程和純電車型，使用8年、行駛16萬公里後電池健康度仍高於75%。 電池安全還包括製造和車輛使用過程中的質量管理：連山電池製造體系設定 9960項質量管控點 ，通過線上CT、X射線及AI視覺檢測記錄關鍵資料，每顆電芯都有獨立電子檔案，製造記錄最長可追溯20年。 車輛交付後，車端、充電樁和雲端繼續監測電池狀態，雲端預警系統可對部分潛在風險提前72小時發出預警。 在這些技術介紹之後，理想正式公佈了 連山電池保障計劃 ，給出兩項終身保障承諾： 第一項是 電池不自燃終身保障 ，因理想自研電池本身質量問題引發自燃且車輛達到報廢標準，理想賠付同等配置的新車。 第二項是 碰撞不起火終身保障 ，因碰撞或底盤剮蹭起火且達到報廢標準，理想補足車損險保單保額與保險實際賠付之間的差額。 自研電驅繼續升級，超充網路擴至4200座 目前，理想已經量產五合一電驅動系統和高壓碳化矽三合一電驅動系統，研發覆蓋電機、電控、功率晶片、材料以及製造工藝。 這次重點介紹了兩項創新。 首先是 CAR119鑄鋁轉子材料 。 理想通過調整轉子材料的微觀結構，使機械強度提高21%、導電能力提升超8%，新一代輔驅電機可使全新L9、L8的城市純電續航增加超15公里，高速續航提升8公里以上。 另一項是 分散式無端子直連技術 。 理想重新設計功率模組，將銅排直接連線到模組基板，距離晶片僅3毫米。 為確保連線可靠，雷射焊接深度偏差控制在100微米以內，歷時四年試製超一萬套樣件。官方稱，相關設計可使新一代電驅增加約30公里續航，並釋放24毫米整車高度空間。 電驅可靠性也在強化。電控零部件數量減少53%、裝配工序減少65%；每臺電驅下線前經過93道質量檢測，並借鑑航空故障預測與健康管理技術，利用23萬輛車的執行資料提前識別故障。 據介紹，自研電驅量產以來，整機故障率改善5.7倍。理想還透露，下一代電驅目標也已確定：系統效率突破94%、功率提升30%、功率密度提升40%。 電池、電驅持續升級，超充網路的建設也沒有停下。 截至此次釋出會，理想已建成 4200座超充站、超過2.3萬根超充樁 ，覆蓋25條國家級高速幹線及138條長途充電風景線。 理想計劃今年底實現國家高速幹線平均每100公里佈局一座超充站，並在 2027年春節前將5C超充槍數量增加至8300根 。 目前，理想超充裝置 最快13秒即可啟動充電 ，裝置可用率超過99.9%；全國超過99.8%的場站支援充電期間免停車費。 除提高充電速度外，理想還通過導航自動規劃、功率排程、低溫提前預熱等功能改善補能耗時，並已投運全車位全自動超充站，使用者無需下車即可完成補能。 至此，連山電動技術體系已經基本完整：電池決定儲能、充電效能和使用壽命，電驅影響能源利用效率，超充網路改善長途出行便利性，研發、製造和車輛使用環節也建立了統一的質量資料體系。 但對於理想來說，這些技術能夠逐步實現量產，還有一個重要前提： 整車企業需要深入掌握核心零部件的研發設計和製造過程。 六年自研之後，理想重新明確供應鏈分工 釋出會前一天，李想專門發了一篇長微博，討論汽車主機廠為什麼要自研電池。 李想認為，一個成熟的產業既需要專業供應商持續創新，也需要整機企業深入研究核心技術——汽車行業 既需要最懂智慧電動車的電池企業，也需要最懂電池的智慧電動車企業。 隨後，李想還透露，理想早在 2020年 就已經決定自研電池，晶片、三電、增程器等核心技術也陸續納入自主研發範圍。 但他同時強調， 自研和合作是不同階段的不同選擇 ，理想不會排斥任何技術領先的供應商。 理想最早研發增程系統時，就發現外購標準零部件的侷限——發動機與發電機的配合、發電效率、噪聲和車輛平順性，都需要針對整車需求專門設計。 純電產品開發進一步提高了這種要求，5C超充需要高倍率電芯和足夠的散熱能力，高壓平臺需要適配的電驅電控系統，充電速度還受充電樁輸出功率和網路佈局影響。 理想選擇深入電芯材料、功率晶片和控制演算法研發，並根據實際需要決定製造方式： 電芯自主研發、合作夥伴代工，磷酸鐵鋰電池包自研自制；功率晶片由理想研發、專業廠商代工，部分功率模組和電驅總成則在自有工廠生產。 自研範圍擴大，並沒有中斷與電池供應商的合作：今年9月，理想宣佈擬斥資 26.5億元增資欣旺達動力 ，此前與寧德時代等專業電池企業也保持著長期合作。 車企加大自研投入、同時繼續投資採購專業供應商的產品，反映雙方分工正在調整：理想掌握技術方案、整車系統設計和關鍵質量資料，專業供應商繼續承擔大量製造工作。 而且，自研未必能夠直接降低成本。馬東輝此前接受媒體採訪時就曾明確表示， 自研電池的綜合成本，不一定低於直接外採。 那麼，理想為什麼仍然願意投入六年時間？ 此次釋出會給出的另一個答案，是 製造與使用資料的完整性 。 傳統產業鏈分工明確，整車企業能拿到供應商的產品效能、檢測結果和質量檔案，卻未必掌握零部件全部製造工序的原始資料。一旦出現質量異常，追溯材料、生產裝置和工藝參數需要跨越多家企業。 理想希望通過深度自研與代工合作，儘可能消除這些資訊隔離。 通過完整的製造資料，理想能夠提前識別生產過程中的細微變化，並與代工廠共同改進。 電池也是類似的邏輯。此次釋出的連山體系，將原材料批次、電芯生產工序、電池包檢測、車輛執行和充電記錄聯絡起來，支援後續故障追溯和風險預測。 這意味著理想參與核心零部件研發之後， 質量管理 可以更深入製造環節，並延續至車輛交付之後。 而對整車企業來說，質量管理本身也有非常現實的教訓。 2025年10月，理想曾因冷卻液防腐效能不足，召回11411輛2024款MEGA，相關車輛在特定條件下存在動力電池熱失控風險。 此次釋出會詳細介紹的防漏液結構、絕緣防護、熱擴散控制和資料預警，正對應這類問題——技術方案需要驗證，規模化製造也必須維持穩定的質量水平。 李想在釋出會當天的微博中也談到，消費者購買電動車，沒必要先成為電池技術專家，剩餘電量準不準、冬季續航怎麼樣、充電需要多久、車輛是否安全、壽命如何保障，都應由整車企業給出答案——車輛的安全、質量、效能和壽命，也應由理想負責。 對理想來說，研發和製造環節掌握得越深入，承擔整車產品責任所需要的技術依據也就越充分。 而放眼汽車產業，這種變化可能還會繼續。動力電池、電驅和功率晶片的研發投入不斷增加，整車廠與供應商圍繞整車設計、製造資料和質量控制的分工更加深入，理想集中展示連山體系正是這一趨勢的縮影。 更大的背景，則是電動汽車技術競爭正在加速。 理想最初選擇增程，主要為了解決純電續航和補能不足的問題，理想ONE和L系列因此獲得市場認可；但如今800V高壓平臺、超快充、大容量電池正在普及，早期依靠增程建立的優勢面臨新的競爭。 技術研發需要更長時間的投入，行業先進水平卻在不斷提高，許多曾經構成差異的技術正成為市場競爭的基礎要求。 對理想來說，連山的釋出意味著多年研發成果進入規模化應用，也意味著下一輪技術升級已經開始。 汽車產業的競爭越來越激烈，維持現有的技術水平和產品競爭力，需要的投入反而越來越多。 因為當所有參與者都在同步加大投入時，行業的基準水平也在不斷抬升。曾經構成產品差異的技術可能會加速變成行業標配；今天的領先優勢，或許很快就會被對手追平。 你必須不停地奔跑，才能保持在原地。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 理想汽車 傑西卡 實探寧德時代總部：“去寧化”是喊太大聲了
