title: Most advice is right for the person giving it
abstract:
Steve Jobs gave a famous speech at Stanford, where he told graduates that the only way to do great work is to love what you do, and that if you haven't found your passion yet, you should keep looking. Interestingly, Mark Cuban says the opposite: don't follow your passion, follow your effort , because you'll end up loving whatever you get good at. Who’s right?! I think they're both right…about themselves. Jobs was obsessive; he only ever did well at things he was obsessed with, so of course that's his rule! Cuban is the kind of person who gets hooked on anything he starts winning at, so that's his. A lot of advice is like this. Two smart people can tell you opposite things, and both can make perfect sense. So how do you work out what actually applies to you? Does this apply to me? Take another common contradiction which contains good advice on each side: “say yes to everything” versus “say no to almost everything.” If your career has gone a bit quiet - you're not getting many opportunities, you're not trying new things, or you're early in your career - saying yes more is likely excellent advice. If you already have ten things going on and can’t give any of them enough attention, the exact opposite is probably better. Engineers see this all the time. One team writes about how microservices saved them, another writes about moving back to a monolith, and each was right for its own team size and problems. When you hear advice or someone tells you to do something: don’t copy the rule, understand why it worked for that person. What problem were they solving? What was true about their situation? Then ask the obvious question: is that true for me too? Don’t assume something that works for someone else is what you’ll enjoy too. This illustration couldn’t be loaded. Open the original image ↗ View larger Side note : That’s also why I think finding out your wiring is super important. The better you understand how you naturally work, what gives you energy, how you make decisions, and what kinds of environments bring out your best, the easier it is to tell when someone else’s advice actually fits you and when it doesn’t. To find out your wiring , take the ~3 minute personality assessment that maps a lot of this for you. It’s built on decades of psychology research, and goes much deeper than the usual four-letter personality stuff. Take the test - it's free Or enter coached.com/quiz in your browser. Start with the boring answer When I’m confused by a lot of different directions, I love to ask: what’s the boring, obvious answer here? Take weight loss. You can spend months debating keto, fasting, meal timing, carbs, exercise routines, etc. But what's the boring answer? Eat less . Everyone already knows this. That's what makes it boring. Which is why I find it pretty funny that Ozempic is arguably the biggest weight-loss breakthrough in decades - and all it does is make you…eat less. Billions in R&D, and the answer was the platitude the whole time. Ha. I find this useful whenever I’m stuck. What’s the simplest answer here? Am I actually doing that? Why not? There's a well-known essay among programmers called "Choose Boring Technology" that makes the same argument for picking tools. Boring advice gets ignored because there’s a whole industry built on advice, and the obvious doesn’t sell :) The older I get, the more I realize the boring platitudes are often the best advice. This illustration couldn’t be loaded. Open the original image ↗ View larger Can I just find out? Here's a habit I've ingrained in myself. You're going to have a lot of people telling you what you should do: do this, try that, you have to be doing X. Instead of taking their word for it or ignoring it, I step back and ask: can I just find out for myself? Can I run a small experiment and get my own answer? Quick example: a lot of content creators say (no surprise) that creating content is the best thing you can do for your career. I could see it working for them, especially for job searching. I just didn't know if it was worth it for me. So I tested it: posted on LinkedIn consistently, grew a decent following, and paid attention to what it actually did for me. My answer: useful, but not useful enough to keep putting the same energy into it. So I'm less active there now and I don’t wonder about it anymore. Get into the habit of testing things out in a small way first! If you’re thinking of switching careers, do a small paid gig at a reduced rate first. If you want to build a company, use AI to make a prototype first and try to market it. Before making any big decision, ask: what could I do that would give me actual data? This illustration couldn’t be loaded. Open the original image ↗ View larger We trust confident people, even when they're wrong The human brain has a pathetic flaw: we routinely mistake confidence for competence. This is proven in the research too. There’s a 2013 study where people rated statements made with high confidence as far more credible, even when the speaker was demonstrably wrong and had no evidence to back it up. When someone speaks with absolute conviction on a podcast or in a boardroom, your own instincts wobble. "They sound so sure. Maybe my read is completely backward." Train yourself to develop an immune response to charismatic certainty. When someone speaks with zero nuance, try to mentally discount their certainty and look at the actual argument underneath. What do they actually know? What evidence do they have? This illustration couldn’t be loaded. Open the original image ↗ View larger Use AI to argue the other side AI can make almost any position sound convincing. Ask whether you should quit your job and it can make a great case for leaving. Ask why you should stay and it can make a great case for that too. A Stanford study published in Science this year found chatbots agreed with people asking for personal advice about 49% more often than humans did. So I find it more useful as a sparring partner than an oracle. If I’m leaning one way, I’ll ask it to make a case for the opposite, point out what I might be assuming, and tell me what information would change the answer. It helps me stay grounded and make up my own mind! This illustration couldn’t be loaded. Open the original image ↗ View larger

title: SCOTUS couldn't take up a copyright case because four justices have book deals
abstract:
The US Supreme Court couldn’t take up a copyright law dispute after four justices with book deals with a party linked to the case declined to participate. The court said Monday that the recusals caused it to lack a quorum to consider a petition brought by BMG Rights Management LLC and other publishers, and that the other five justices agreed the case couldn’t be heard this term. The case would have addressed whether creators exercising their right to terminate deals signing away their rights decades later could include foreign rights. The answer to the question the court declined to definitively answer carries massive implications for the valuation of any works like music or movie franchises with global markets spanning decades. With the Fifth Circuit bucking a long-running consensus by finding creators can reclaim foreign rights, the outcome will impact valuations, generate litigation, and spur forum-shopping, attorneys said. “It’s going to have a real impact on the business side of things because of the ambiguity as to whether those future rights can be recaptured,” entertainment IP attorney David Gold of Cole Schotz said. “It’s going to be a race to the courthouse.” The court disclosed that Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Neil Gorsuch, Amy Coney Barrett, and Ketanji Brown Jackson took no part in the consideration of the petition. The justices didn’t offer reasons for their decision, but BMG Rights is owned by Bertelsmann SE, a German media conglomerate that also owns Penguin Random House, the US publishing giant that has published books authored by those four justices. That includes publishing memoirs by Jackson and Barrett in 2024 and 2025, respectively. The Supreme Court didn’t immediately respond to a request for further comment on the recusals. Book publishing has proved to be a lucrative endeavor for the justices, with all but two having authored a book or signed contracts to do so. Monday’s announcement shows how those activities can have far-reaching consequences, keeping the court from considering a dispute prompting sharp disagreements in the lower courts. “I don’t think I’ve ever seen a statutorty affirmance by default, ever,” Gold said. Courts Split In declining to take up BMG Right’s Management’s petition, the court affirmed a lower court ruling that Cyril Vetter, who co-wrote the 1960s song “Double Shot (Of My Baby’s Love),” could and had reclaimed worldwide rights to the song. Vetter had previously convinced a court that by treaty, the country closest to the work determines ownership while enforcement hinges on law where it happens. “IP landscape-wise, we have a problem,” IP law professor Philippa Loengard of Columbia University said of courts’ divergent views. “It’s going to lead to a lot more litigation as creators attempt to reclaim rights abroad, and a lot more effort by creators to get Vetter rationale accepted in other circuits.” District courts in the US Courts of Appeals for the Ninth and Second circuits have rejected recovery of assigned foreign rights with US law leading to an industry consensus. BMG also argued the Second Circuit itself presented a definite split. But the Fifth Circuit ruling — which attorneys deemed “a shock” but also “very well-reasoned” — rejected that reasoning based on its interpretation of the Berne Convention, an international copyright treaty to which the US is a party. The opinion also said the Second Circuit opinion didn’t address the precise question at issue. Termination rights allow creators to nullify assignments generally 35 to 40 years after they sign away the rights at issue. They were designed to help creators who often give up their rights before their true value was known, often from a poor bargaining position. Vetter in 2019 began seeking termination of his assignment of rights to the song made famous in performances by the Swingin’ Medallions and Dick Holler And The Holidays. Resnik Music Group, which acquired the song, argued it retained the rights after the termination became effective in 2022. The US District Court for the Middle District of Louisiana granted Vetter’s motion for summary judgment, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed . In the Berne Convention, 181 countries agreed to recognize an original copyright, not create new parallel rights with independent fates, it reasoned. BMG and other related entities acquired Resnik’s interest in the song, and substituted themselves as the plaintiff in March. Music, movie, and photo industry groups filed amicus briefs supporting BMG’s position and arguing the court should take up the case. Monday’s decision marks at least the second time that the court lacked a quorum in a case connected to Bertelsmann SE. In May 2025, Alito joined Sotomayor, Gorsuch, Barrett, and Jackson in not participating in a case linked to the company. Alito published his first book, So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court and Our Country , earlier this year under Basic Books’ Basic Liberty imprint. The case is BMG Rights Mgmt. LLC v. Vetter, U.S., No. 25-1391, affirmed 10/19/26. title: People sick of being spied on by their smart TV
abstract:
‘It’s not intimidating, just increasingly enshittified’ … a user and their smart TV. Photograph: SimpleImages/Getty Images View image in fullscreen ‘It’s not intimidating, just increasingly enshittified’ … a user and their smart TV. Photograph: SimpleImages/Getty Images ‘It was so satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen’: the people sick of being spied on by their smart TV Is your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacy W hen Dan had had enough of his television, he threw a rock straight through the screen. The offence? His smart TV was downloading its third update in three days. “It drove me crazy with what seemed like daily software updates that never fixed anything and ‘features’ that never seemed to work,” says the 71-year-old from Illinois. “And of course, constantly trying to push me to subscribe to paid-for services when all I wanted to do was watch over-the-air TV, play a DVD or stream something from my computer.” Some may accuse Dan of being a luddite, but his master’s degree in computer science and decades of experience in telecommunications would suggest otherwise. “The tech is not intimidating,” he explains, “just increasingly enshittified .” The first smart TVs entered the market in the late 2000s, when companies introduced operating systems, media players and apps to screens that were becoming wider and thinner. In recent years, the luxury status of smart TVs has waned and increasingly affordable options are widely available. Tom Parsons, TV and audiovisual editor at the electronics magazine What Hi-Fi?, explains that these cheaper models can struggle under more advanced features. “They’re not necessarily super-fast and responsive out of the box,” he says. “And then two, three, four years down the line, they can end up slowing down quite a lot under the weight of all that processing.” Dan is just one of a growing number of tech-savvy watchers wishing their TVs weren’t so smart. Erin McQuiston and Matthew Schroyer, a couple from Connecticut, share his smart-screen scepticism. View image in fullscreen Increasingly hard to find … a dumb TV. Photograph: Svetlana Lazarenka/Alamy “I don’t think we’ve ever used [our TV] as anything other than just a giant display,” says McQuiston. “There was a period where we were running it through an Xbox. And that was a constant battle because that was constantly being updated and patched and then you’d have to redownload all the apps for it.” Meanwhile, Schroyer says his job as a software engineer has influenced his decision to “intentionally keep it very dumb” by keeping their TV disconnected from the internet. “A rule of the house is: don’t give things the wifi password,” he says. “It concerns me that folks increasingly have to be IT experts to get the bare minimum enjoyable experience out of this stuff.” Instead, the 41-year-old connects his screen to an Apple TV box as a streaming workaround, and cites privacy as well as “highly invasive” advertisements for doing so. “Our living room is not a billboard for sale,” he says. When asked how the couple might cope in a future where TVs may have mandatory internet, McQuiston says her husband is “handy enough to break every terms of service known to man and get in there and unsolder something to manually disconnect it”. For Helen Northmore, a 51-year-old from Wales who works in AI delivery for the UK Health Security Agency, privacy is also a worry. Her grudge against smart screens began four years ago, when her faithful dumb TV broke without warning and she had to quickly find a replacement. “We had already decided that we didn’t want the smart functionality, but it became really clear that it was very hard to find one that didn’t have any,” she says. Northmore, whose partner works in cybersecurity, says the couple wanted to “keep control” over their devices, which cost them a premium. “We were willing to pay more. One of the boundaries in how we live our lives is we want to minimise the smart element. We don’t have smart speakers. We don’t enable or connect to the internet.” View image in fullscreen ‘Our living room is not a billboard for sale’ … a smart TV aerial. Photograph: Zdenek Maly/Alamy Today, she watches entertainment through a Sky box connected to her dumb TV, and dreads that when her current telly breaks there won’t be any option but to get a smart model and offer up her data. More consumers are becoming worried about how their information is being used by manufacturers. “There are increasing privacy concerns around to what degree TVs are essentially scraping your data,” says Parsons. “TVs these days are full of sensors, including microphones, and that can make people nervous.” But according to Parsons, despite interest in “dumber” models from some buyers, most shoppers want their TVs to be catch-all entertainment systems. The result is that the dumb TV market is almost nonexistent. “You can buy cheap monitors for signage,” he says, “but from a features point of view, you wouldn’t get the same performance that you would from a consumer TV.” Paul, a public servant from Australia, knows just how hard finding a traditional TV can be. “When my last telly – a glorious 32-inch dumb TV – died recently, aged approximately 10 years old, I spent about three weeks scouring the city looking for something comparable. What I found is that they do not exist any more.” After much searching, Paul discovered a single 40-inch TV without any smart functionality in the back of a shop. “It had zero ways to connect to the internet – just a couple of plugs on the back for making it work with the aerial on the roof and my VHS player, and that was it.” He remembers that it “was very dusty and cost about 200 dollars. Naturally, we fell instantly in love.” “My friends all laugh at it when they come over,” he admits, “but secretly I know the joke is on them. My little telly doesn’t spy on me, and has a DVD player built in.” The punchline may eventually land on Paul, however. In September, the Australian government launched a consultation into the future of the country’s free-to-air broadcasting , asking citizens for feedback on how TV should be accessed. One of the proposed scenarios would see traditional broadcast services cut in favour of streaming services and video on-demand apps. View image in fullscreen ‘My little telly doesn’t spy on me’ … some users such as Paul are clinging hard to analogue. Photograph: Dmitriy Shironosov/Alamy In the same month, the UK government released a media green paper outlining its plan to fully move away from digital terrestrial television to services provided over a broadband connection by 2034 at the earliest. Such a situation would mean viewers having to rely on broadcaster apps and streaming services. If a similar fate befell North America, James certainly wouldn’t care. He is originally from the US but now lives in British Columbia, Canada, and says traditional broadcast TV is “dead to him” and that he prefers to watch shows on streaming services or on YouTube. For the father and husband, privacy is a top priority. “No one expects an end-user licence agreement to include giving up autonomy,” he says. “Having my TV listen to any conversation and use that for monetary or any form of gain is above and beyond expectations on the loss of privacy.” In September, the YouTube channel Gamers Nexus released a two-hour investigation into LG Electronics’ smart televisions, saying that the devices record audio – even when they are offline or powered down. The South Korean company denied the allegations . In the fallout, some have taken measures to modify their smart TVs, regardless of brand or model. Some videos online show users replacing motherboards , cutting out Bluetooth and wifi modules and removing microphones from their TV remote controls.

title: Using Claude to reduce the attack surface of code
abstract:
Chris Rohlf Over the past year, we’ve published lots of data that shows that frontier AI models are more than capable of discovering and exploiting security vulnerabilities. Showing how previously unknown vulnerabilities might be exploited is, however, only the start of what frontier AI models can do for cyber defense. In this post, we summarize some of our initial research into automated attack surface analysis and reduction: the process of using AI models to map the code that is reachable, then removing or restricting access to anything than a given deployment doesn’t need to expose. Automated attack surface analysis and reduction can meaningfully improve the security of deployed software in the near term. Securing software by finding and fixing individual vulnerabilities alone scales poorly: fixing even a critical vulnerability tells you nothing about the vulnerabilities that remain. By contrast, reducing code reachability can reduce the severity of unknown vulnerabilities, including the ones that might be under active exploitation. These techniques don’t remove the unknown vulnerabilities in the code, but they do make the vulnerabilities harder to reach, and thereby reduce their severity. Minimizing codebases’ attack surface results in better security without ever having to find or fix an individual vulnerability. Below, we preview some of the data we’ve collected from applying attack surface reduction techniques to large open-source codebases using Claude. Our aim in doing so is to show that Claude can meaningfully, and economically, improve software security through the methods we outline. Specifically, we ran Claude over 25 projects (in a variety of languages), and it discovered 493 issues. With these results in mind, we discuss how developers can apply similar techniques to their own code. Methods for reducing codebases’ attack surface Over time, software has a tendency to become more complicated, with new layers of abstractions, new dependencies, and new features slowly piling on top of one-another. This can often cause it to function very differently to how its original developers intended. And it is a big part of why attackers are often so successful: they study exactly how a piece of code behaves in practice, rather than how its developers intended or designed it to work. Automated attack surface analysis and reduction techniques aim to discover unnecessary attack surfaces, then move that code behind an appropriate gate. This might involve moving code from pre-authentication to post-authentication, from 0-click to 1-click, from on-by-default to explicit opt-in, or from the first message of a protocol to deeper in the session state machine. Some code is meant to be reachable before these stages, but a lot it is not, and, given the complexity that comes with code churn across thousands or millions of lines of code, unnecessary exposure of features often goes unnoticed. There are numerous ways to reduce the attack surface of code. In our own research efforts, we focused on three methods in particular: Default configuration. We identified code that was reachable in its shipped default configuration but wasn’t intended to be used by any default functionality. Configuration interaction. We found pairs of options that looked reasonable on their own, but which caused issues when configured together (for instance, by silently disabling a security control, or leaving a features behavior undefined while its code remains reachable). Early reachability. We identified security sensitive and complex code that runs either before an appropriate security control (such as authentication), without victim interaction, or before a protocol state transition. We wanted to understand how well Claude could take these three descriptions of attack surface and discover real issues in large and complex codebases. We analyzed 25 open source projects (representing over five million lines of code), written in languages including C, C++, Java, PHP, and Python. Claude created an inventory of over 17,000 configuration options across these projects. Of those, 3,842 related to the configuration of a control or feature that was security relevant. For the purposes of our research, we broke down these open source projects into three broad categories: Public . These projects are built to serve any user who can reach them, or to consume data authored by parties they cannot identify. (Examples include a DNS resolver parsing upstream answers, or a proxy parsing origin responses.) Gated . These projects are intended to serve authenticated users (such as those with a password, key or certificate holders, or enrolled devices). The software still allows for arbitrary client requests, but no functionality is available until the user has been authenticated. Private . These are built and deployed to serve the operator's own private environment. In these cases, adding a control like an authentication layer is optional, but outside the scope of the software. These categories help to contextualize our results. For example, we’d expect a significant percentage of a Public codebase to be reachable in the default configuration (since it’s designed to serve any user), but the opposite to be true for projects in the Gated category. Claude’s findings Claude found 493 issues using the three methods described above. Several themes stuck out to us from its results. First, Claude found that all eleven gated projects had code that was unintentionally reachable (although this code wasn’t a significant percentage of the total lines of code for any of those projects). Specifically, Claude discovered 93 unnecessary pre-authentication surfaces in the default configuration of the gated cohort, 37 locations where code executed, or state was recorded, before authentication, and 61 configuration combinations that silently weakened a pre-authentication control configured by the administrator. None of these issues would have been immediately exploitable on their own, but they create a much larger attack surface than is necessary. A breakdown of issues discovered per category for each technique. Of the 25 projects we assessed, 10 were Public, 11 Gated, and 4 Private. The Gated cohort contained the most surprising results with a high number of early reachability findings. Second, Claude’s work mitigating configuration interaction issues produced some of the most interesting and impactful findings (across all project types). Claude found 162 security sensitive configuration combinations that were accepted both without an error or warning and without any documentation of the expected behavior of their interaction. In 94 of those cases, the combination silently turned off a security control. The other 68 cases were inconsistencies in the same security mechanisms (e.g. a listener or login path would remain reachable even though the configuration would say it was disabled; two settings would conflict, and the one that would take precedence would depend on their order in the configuration file, or a protection configured by the administrator would do nothing while its code remained reachable). While some of these configuration combinations might be non-standard or infrequently used, there would be nothing preventing an administrator of these projects from configuring and deploying the code in this way. Claude also found one specific pattern that turned up independently in four unrelated projects. This would work as follows. An administrator would write an access rule for remote clients using a hostname or a wildcard pattern, instead of an IP address. When a client connects, the server would compare that rule against the client’s hostname. Whether the server ever learned that hostname would depend on a separate option that controlled reverse DNS lookups (which most projects had configured off). With lookups off, the server would only have the client’s IP address.

title: The hidden learning cost of generative AI: the THINK framework for preserving critical thinking in AI-enabled workplaces
abstract:
This paper examines how regular use of generative AI enhances productivity, but somehow, in contrast, reduces the opportunities for employees to utilize critical thinking skills and translate their hands-on experience into organizational learning.
 
 
 
 The paper is a problem-based conceptual synthesis linking AI literacy, organizational learning, human-AI collaboration, evidence from knowledge workers, and knowledge collapse theory. On the other hand, human-AI augmentation and disengagement are considered opposing risks from which five workplace safeguards are derived.
 
 
 
 The paper shows that the issue is not the use of GenAI, but organizations that reward flawless automation output while ignoring verification, human reasoning, and visible employee learning. The paper introduces the THINK framework interlinking organizational practices: Transparency, Human judgment, Intellectual engagement, Navigation of evidence and Knowledge construction.
 
 
 
 The THINK framework conceptual synthesis is selective and not empirically tested. Future research should validate the application effect across different sectors, industries and levels of GenAI adoption.
 
 
 
 The THINK framework can be integrated into employee training, performance management discussions, decision-making and AI governance systems.
 
 
 
 The paper transposes the traditional argument about GenAI-mediated cognition into a simple, auditable framework that managers can apply on the job as coaches, learning professionals, and AI governance teams.

title: Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two Measured Preconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement
abstract: Agent platforms are starting to improve their own agents: they read a deployed agent's execution traces, derive a change, have an automated verifier approve it, and release it with no human author. How much of this loop can safely run without a human? We propose two quantities a platform can measure. Verifier strength $\sigma$ is how well the available verifier -- often an LLM judge -- agrees with a trusted reference verifier; it limits how much a step can improve the agent. Recoverability is how cheaply a bad change can be undone: whether undoing it needs a new verifier approval, and how much of the old behavior a rollback restores. A step should run unattended only if both are adequate. On our platform this rule allows prompt, tool and skill edits to run unattended and keeps weight updates under human sign-off. Our main contribution is these two definitions and how to measure them. We built a platform that applies the rule and tested it in two ways: on the platform's own approval gate, and in controlled experiments on the $\tau^2$-bench agent benchmark. On verifier strength, the platform's LLM judge sometimes gave the same score no matter what it was shown (9 of 37 settings) and reported no error, so a verifier can look healthy while approving anything; its strength must be measured, and two simple tests catch the failure. On recoverability, restoring a saved copy brought the agent back to its original behavior, but a regenerated undo did not, so only changes whose old version is kept can be reversed without a human; and while a change was deployed, it altered the outcome of 17 percent of tasks beyond normal run-to-run variation, which no undo repairs. Together these support the rule: a change can run unattended only when its old version is kept and its verifier's strength has been measured.

title: A Semi-Analytical Inference Framework for Structural Causal Models
abstract: Structural Causal Models (SCMs) provide a principled framework for observational, interventional, and counterfactual reasoning, all of which rely on probabilistic inference. Existing frameworks either transform SCMs into alternative tractable representations or rely on approximate inference with expressive generative models. We instead perform inference using a message passing scheme directly on the SCM by representing structural mechanisms and probability densities in a common finite-dimensional function space. Forward propagation combines a numerical realization of the Law of the Unconscious Statistician, while propagated densities are recovered by spline projection from LOTUS moments. The same representation naturally yields backward message passing for conditioning, providing a unified framework for causal inference. Using tensor-product B-spline bases, the resulting algorithm expresses inference through numerical quadrature and linear algebra without explicitly constructing conditional distributions. Experiments on randomly generated continuous SCMs demonstrate accurate approximation of Monte Carlo reference solutions and systematic improvement with increasing basis resolution.

title: E8-QAT: Efficient 2-Bit Quantization-Aware Training with Implicit Lattice Codebooks
abstract: Low-bit quantization reduces the memory footprint of large language models, but preserving accuracy with efficient training remains challenging. Scalar quantization encodes weights independently, while explicit-codebook vector quantization introduces costly search during training. We propose E8-QAT, a 2-bit quantization-aware training framework that uses the $E_8$ lattice as an implicit eight-dimensional codebook. It jointly quantizes weight groups through arithmetic projection without storing or searching an explicit codebook during the training forward pass. A 2-bit core encoding and sparse extension preserve the selected lattice points exactly, adding less than 0.1\% to core index storage. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, E8-QAT matches the performance of the full-precision model in terms of the average score across the four tasks. E8-QAT improves over the state-of-the-art baseline by 2.03\% on IFEval and by 1.51\% on LiveCodeBench, under the same data, schedule, and bit width. The 2-bit representation reduces peak memory by 80\% and supports a $4\times$ larger batch. At each representation's largest feasible batch, E8-QAT reaches $1.97\times$ the decoding throughput of BF16.

title: Human enough? Examining morality and ethical perceptions of service robots
abstract:
This study examines how robot-related social and humanlike cues shape consumers' perceived morality and perceived ethics of service robots, and how these appraisals impact trust and intention to use.
 
 
 
 A total of 257 usable surveys were collected from diners who have engaged with a service robot at a fine dining restaurant. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM).
 
 
 
 A robot's perceived mind of its own and social presence significantly influenced consumers' perceived morality and perceived ethics. Perceived ethics and social presence significantly influenced trust, while perceived morality and mind of its own exhibited nonsignificant effects on trust. Trust strongly predicted intention to use. Mediation analysis confirmed the intermediary effects of trust between social presence, perceived ethics and intention to use.
 
 
 
 The findings suggest that managers should balance robot autonomy with predictability, prioritize ethical transparency over simulated moral reasoning, design social presence carefully and treat trust-building as an operational process involving reliability, service recovery and escalation protocols.
 
 
 
 The study contributes to service robot research by distinguishing perceived morality as consumers' attribution of moral capacity from perceived ethics as consumers' evaluation of ethical conduct. It further shows that moral and ethical appraisals do not translate into trust in identical ways, highlighting the need to understand service robot acceptance through moral cognition, ethical evaluation and trust formation.

title: COMPASS: Routing via Capability-Oriented Model Profiling with Adaptive Search, Selection, and Tool Use
abstract: LLM routing aims to select a capable model at low cost, but specialized routers can require updates as models and tasks change. We propose COMPASS, an agentic router in which an LLM follows a routing recipe, gathers performance and cost evidence through tools, and optionally inspects candidate answers before selecting a model. Our evaluations on LLMRouterBench and DeepSWE show that agentic routing can improve accuracy and lower model-call cost relative to specialized and trained routing baselines, without routing-specific training. On LLMRouterBench, COMPASS reaches 69.85% accuracy at \$139.57, compared with RLCascadeRouter's 69.14% at \$180.22. On DeepSWE under fixed five-fold cross-validation, it reaches 78.1% at \$215, compared with 74.1% at \$500 for the best single model. COMPASS also supports routing across benchmarks and adapts to an expanded model pool by reading new evaluation records, without changing the router's weights or prompt.

title: Robot-Task Suitability in Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Task Allocation
abstract: Heterogeneous multi-robot task allocation depends on estimates of how suitable individual robots are for candidate tasks, yet suitability can be defined in substantially different ways. We compare ten deterministic methods and two LLM-based variants spanning rule-based, similarity-based, requirement-oriented, fuzzy, and semantic approaches. Using common robot and task profiles, we compare how the methods score and rank candidate robots, identify feasibility, and select a top robot, while examining how these outcomes change with team composition, scale, spatial context, capability uncertainty, and task representation. The methods frequently disagree despite operating on identical scenarios. Generic similarity measures can violate properties expected under a one-sided requirement-satisfaction interpretation of suitability, while LLM-based scoring introduces additional stochastic and linguistic sensitivity. These results show that robot--task suitability should be treated as an explicit modeling choice whose assumptions, robustness, and decision-level consequences should be considered before allocation.

title: Ask to Distill: Learning to Synthesize Data for On-Policy Distillation
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) can succeed with surprisingly few training questions, motivating a view of questions as carriers of distributional knowledge transfer. How can we assess whether a newly generated question is valuable for distillation, and learn to generate better questions---without access to its correct answer? We introduce Ask-to-Distill (\method), a framework that treats synthetic questions as distribution elicitors and optimizes the teacher supervision they expose along student-generated trajectories. A student-initialized synthesizer is optimized using a distributional surrogate for question value, computed from a frozen student--teacher pair without reference answers, correctness rewards, or per-candidate student updates. The reward combines teacher--student disagreement with teacher probability mass on the student's candidate support, together with length and diversity controls. The generated questions are filtered and deduplicated into a prompt-only bank for standard OPD. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and agentic tasks, our method improves average performance and teacher-gap recovery over unoptimized student-generated prompts and KL-filtered real questions, while matching or exceeding real-bank OPD in the evaluated settings. Signal analyses further show that optimized questions can elicit denser supervision and more total signal from shorter student responses, supporting elicited distributional supervision as an objective for synthetic distillation data. Our code, data and models are publicly available at https://github.com/GasolSun36/Ask_to_Distill.

title: TrajEvolve: Trajectory Evolution for Reinforcement Learning with Hindsight Credit Assignment
abstract: The Reinforcement Learning (RL) paradigm has achieved remarkable success in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, when applied to long-horizon tasks, it faces severe challenges: i) Due to the high task complexity, the model struggles to sample enough successful trajectories, resulting in slow convergence. ii) Relying solely on sparse final rewards causes all steps to be updated indiscriminately, encouraging redundant step generation. When both the quantity and quality of successful trajectories become difficult to guarantee, the performance is severely constrained. This dilemma stems from the limitations: existing RL paradigms rely entirely on the reasoning capability of base models, lacking the ability to actively optimize trajectories. To address the above issues, we propose a novel trajectory evolution paradigm with hindsight credit assignment, termed TrajEvolve. TrajEvolve not only relies on the trajectory inferred by the model but also generates ``evolutionary trajectories''by refining low-quality steps in historical trajectories, thereby exposing the policy to high-quality compositions that lie within the base model's support but are rarely sampled within practical training budgets. Furthermore, TrajEvolve reformulates step-level continuous credit assignment as a binary classification task, whether each step is necessary for task completion. This simplification not only reduces the learning difficulty but also enables step labels to be obtained through counterfactual verification, achieving precise identification of redundant steps. Extensive experiments on two datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method.

title: DIVE: Benchmarking Full-Duplex Interaction with Visual Engagement in Continuous Streams
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially improved spoken interaction and video understanding. Existing online and streaming benchmarks primarily assess causal multimodal perception through timestamped question answering, whereas real-world interaction requires models to continuously identify task-relevant multimodal cues and decide whether, when, and how to respond. This leaves open how well current models can sustain real-time interaction throughout an evolving multimodal stream. To address this gap, we introduce DIVE, a benchmark for evaluating full-duplex interaction with visual engagement under continuous and realistic multimodal streams. It organizes six tasks into three complementary interaction scenarios. (1) Proactive Intervention evaluates whether models can identify emerging visual or semantic cues and intervene at the appropriate moment. (2) Continuous Engagement evaluates sustained participation through continuous visual tracking and visually grounded query interaction. (3) Interaction Coordination evaluates how models coordinate listening and speaking under overlapping and multi-party interactions. DIVE contains 525 audio/video samples with fine-grained human annotations and precise temporal metadata. Its evaluation protocol separates response quality, participation decisions, and response timing. We evaluate representative real-time models using response quality, window response rates, and reaction latency. Experiments show that leading real-time models achieve sub-second average response latency, yet their average window response rates remain at or below 53.77%. Response quality varies substantially across models and tasks, with adapting ongoing responses to newly arriving information remaining particularly challenging. We hope DIVE facilitates progress toward more natural and capable real-time multimodal interactive systems.

title: Local Inference of LLMs on Long Contexts: A Data Systems Perspective
abstract: Large language models can solve complex problems across a variety of subjects, such as mathematics and coding. For such complex analytical tasks, models with a long context perform better. Serving models with long context is currently mostly done on powerful systems with multiple GPUs, which are too expensive for most users. An alternative is local inference, or serving a model on a user's own machine, which removes per-token costs and rate limits, besides keeping sensitive data private and giving users full control over the models they run. The common understanding, however, is that local LLMs need compression (e.g., quantization) to run on a single GPU. In this paper, we set out to study the limitations that prevent serving long-context models for single users, besides the capacity issue. Rather than characterizing a single model on one GPU, we analyze how different models behave across several GPU generations. This lets us uncover not just individual bottlenecks but broader trends in where inefficiencies arise. Our analysis confirms that, as expected, self-attention dominates the runtime for long-context inference. More unexpectedly, our evaluation reveals that the current structure of self-attention leaves key GPU resources significantly underutilized, and the newest GPU is often the least well served. Many of these findings are fundamentally data management problems, from paging the KV cache to improving cache utilization and synchronization in the GPU, which is why we bring this study to the Data Systems community. To engage this community, we present our findings as a series of experimental observations and formulate recommendations for future work.

title: Standards-Guided and Dependency-Aware Code-Level Documentation Generation
abstract: Automatically generating high-quality documentation for software repositories remains challenging: existing approaches largely treat documentation as unconstrained text generation, lacking explicit quality specifications, depending heavily on long-context prompts over raw code, and offering limited support for reproducible evaluation. We argue that code-level documentation generation should instead be a standards-guided software engineering task, in which documentation is generated and assessed against explicit, reusable quality requirements derived from authoritative standards. We define code documentation as natural-language descriptions of repository functions and classes, organized by source-code path. We present CODEDOC, a standards-guided and dependency-aware framework that identifies dependencies between code entities via static call-graph and AST analysis and constructs dependency-aware structured prompts combining local code context, repository paths, and documentation criteria drawn from authoritative standards and style guides. We further introduce an interactive LLM-as-a-judge protocol that supplies criterion-aligned feedback to refine generated documentation along fine-grained dimensions from formal and practice-oriented standards. Experiments on ten open-source Python repositories show that CODEDOC produces higher-quality documentation than RepoAgent and a long-context baseline under standards-aligned evaluation, with relative improvements of 11.6%-17.0% and 21.4%-29.6%, respectively, while consuming roughly an order of magnitude fewer tokens per documentation entity than the long-context baseline. A human study confirms substantial alignment between LLM-based and human judgments (Spearman's rho = 0.72), and the relative findings hold across different judge LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/ControllableModel/CodeDoc.
